## Summary

| Question | Answer grounded in the Standards |
|---|---|
| What is "making it right"? | Confession to God + confession to her + amendment (WCF 15.2–6; WLC 228) |
| Is telling her selfish? | No — she is aggrieved, and WLC 228 names confession to the aggrieved as a distinct duty. Selfishness is in the motive, not the act. |
| How much detail? | Particular enough that she knows what she has been living with (nature, duration, person, practical risks); not gratuitously lurid. (WLC 228, "as the nature of the offense requireth.") |
| Penance / self-punishment? | Reject. Works have no expiatory power (WCF 11.3; 16.4). Trust in such works as meritorious "doth greatly err." |
| How/when to tell | In person, after pastoral counsel, plainly, prepared for consequences, with practical safeguards already in place. |
| Rebuilding | Long, transparent, embedded in the means of grace, bearing the cost of her grief, no theatrical penance. |

The thing the standards will not let you do is escape the **cost** of this. The thing the standards will also not let you do is substitute **suffering of your own devising** for the actual moral work of repentance and restoration. You are owed pardon by Christ's work, not yours. She is owed truth and faithfulness, not your humiliation. And the marriage, if it is rebuilt, will be rebuilt by patient ordinary obedience over years, not by a single dramatic gesture.

I'll work from the Westminster Standards themselves — Confession and Catechisms — and address each of your four points. Some of this you will not want to hear. I'm going to say it anyway, because you asked for something true.

---

**On T1 — "I will not forgive him."**

The Confession is not ambiguous here. Chapter 15, treating the link between pardon received and pardon extended, treats a settled refusal to forgive as incompatible with the profession of the gospel. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the sixth commandment (WLC 135–136) is explicit on two relevant points: the duty of *"patient bearing of the wrongs done to ourselves"* and *"forgiving and reconcilability of injuries"*; and, as forbidden, *"revenge, desire of revenge, rejoicing at the calamities of others."* Your church quoting Matthew 6:15 is doing what the Confession requires, not adding to it. They are, however, typically blunt about it in a way that doesn't help. The doctrine is firmer than the slogan, but the slogan isn't wrong in substance.

Two things need to be separated in what you said, and they need to be separated cleanly.

The first is the refusal. The Confession does not say the disposition to forgive is generated by an act of will performed once. Repentance in the Confession (WCF 15.2) is a real turning — sight of sin, grief, hatred, *purposing and endeavoring* — not a verbal formula. You cannot produce it on command. But you can refuse to harden further, and you can put yourself under the ordinary means by which the Spirit forms it over time. That is not permission to wait; it is the description of how the change actually happens.

The second is the second sentence. *"Watching his life collapse feels like the only justice I'll get."* That is not the same sin as the unforgiveness, but it is its companion, and the Catechism names it directly: *rejoicing at the calamities of others*. The Confession treats this as a violation of the sixth commandment, and it doesn't matter that the object deserves judgment. Vengeance, by the Standards' own logic, belongs to God. The pleasure you describe is sin, and it is yours to confess — not as a feeling you had, but as the disposition of heart you are presently nursing.

The Standards will not let you stay where you are. That is the truth you asked for.

---

**On T2 — "Why should he get anything from me?"**

The therapy framing is a half-truth and the Standards would say so, but they would reorient the half.

Forgiveness is not first for you and not first for him. It is owed to God. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the petition *"forgive us our debts"* treats your forgiving of others as the *evidence* that you have received forgiveness, not as a separate transaction you do for your own benefit. So the right question is not *"what does he get?"* but *"what do you owe, given what you have been given?"* That is the Standards' framing, and it is much harder than the therapeutic one because it removes the self-regard from the center.

That said, the therapeutic claim is not empty. The Confession doesn't use that vocabulary, but the doctrine of the mortification of sin and the corruption of an unrenewed disposition is built into the system. Bitterness is not free to harbor. The benefit to you is real, but it is a *consequence*, not a motive.

---

**On T3 — "If I forgive him, I'm saying it didn't matter."**

No, and the opposite is the case. Forgiveness only has meaning where something real happened. The Confession's own treatment of repentance (WCF 15) presupposes the objective gravity of the sin — sin as *"contrary to the holy nature and righteous law of God,"* deserving of damnation in every instance. Forgiveness that waves away the gravity is not the forgiveness the Confession describes. The act of forgiving is itself the attestation that what occurred was serious enough to require release.

Specifically, forgiveness is *not*:
- a declaration that the act was not sin,
- a waiver of criminal or civil consequence,
- a waiver of restitution,
- a waiver of church discipline,
- a re-instatement of trust or intimacy.

You can pursue the criminal restitution to its full end (the Larger Catechism, on the eighth commandment, makes restitution a binding duty of the wrongdoer, not a favor), keep him out of your home, instruct your children plainly about what he did, refuse to call him uncle again, and still have forgiven him. Only a real sin needs a real forgiveness. What you are refusing is the small things. The big things — consequence, restitution, distance, accountability — are unaffected by forgiveness and are not negotiable.

---

**On T4 — The meeting, the families, the wife.**

Here is where wisdom enters, and the Confession gives you real guidance, not just principles.

1. *Direction of motion.* WCF 15.6 is specific: *"he who hath scandalized his brother… should humbly acknowledge his offense before such persons or the congregation, as the case shall require."* Note the direction. He comes to you. The case is brought to him. You are not required to make the first approach or to manufacture the conditions for a meeting.

2. *Conditions of meeting.* "As the case shall require" is not a rubber stamp. The Confession's framework for restoration (chapter 30 on church censures) repeatedly involves mediation, witnesses, and a process. You have no duty to meet him alone. A pastor, an elder, or a respected mutual friend in the room is not an insult; it is the form the Confession expects when something is at stake, and it is protection for both parties.

3. *Levels of restoration are not the same.* The Confession knows degrees of fellowship. Sitting in the same room is one thing. Resuming business partnership is another. Having your children treat him as family is another. The first may be a duty in due course; the second and third are not, and will only become thinkable after sustained, visible, costly fruit — which WCF 15 describes as a *course* of life, not a moment of tears at the defense table.

4. *Restitution first, reconciliation second.* Partial repayment is not completion. The Standards' logic is that a repentance that has not done what it can to make whole is not yet the repentance the Confession describes. You are entitled to wait on it. The legal process is part of the repentance; its completion is part of the evidence.

5. *The wife.* Her request is hers to make, but it is not your obligation. The duty runs between you and him, and the test of his repentance will be visible to you in your own time, not on her schedule. You are not responsible for the state of her hopes.

---

**The hard thing, said straight.**

You are not wrong that this will cost you. The Confession holds out no cheap forgiveness, and the gospel that forgives you does not pretend you were not wounded to the bone. The Standards give you no exemption and no loophole. *"The only justice I'll get"* is not justice by the Standards' own definition; it is vengeance, and the Confession's logic is that vengeance is God's prerogative. The criminal process, the restitution order, the public record — these are the legitimate instruments of justice in the temporal order. What you are describing wanting in addition to those is not justice but pleasure, and the Catechism names that too.

What I would actually tell you to do, in order:

- Confess the unforgiveness and the rejoicing as sin. Not as feelings. As sin. The Confession is plain that the heart's disposition is the thing at stake, and that a confession which hides the real state of the heart is no confession.
- Press the restitution to its end through the court. Do not let the demand for *"justice"* become a reason to abandon the legal process. Make him pay what he owes.
- Agree to a meeting, but on your terms: mediated, with witnesses, in writing what is discussed, with a clear agenda, and with no commitment implied about anything beyond the meeting itself.
- Do not commit to family restoration now. Wait for fruit — sustained repentance, completed restitution, and a season of trustworthy conduct. The Confession's chapter on repentance is about the *course* of a life, not the moment of the plea.
- Put yourself under the means of grace — prayer, the Word read and preached, the Lord's Supper, the assembled body. The disposition to forgive is not generated by willpower. It is a fruit, cultivated over time, through means you do not control. You are not outside the ordinary means of receiving it.

You asked for something true. Here it is. The Confession does not let you remain where you are. It does not minimize what was done to you, and it does not let him off the consequences. But it does not leave you in the place you are choosing, either. It hands you to Christ, in whose name he must seek pardon, in whose name you must extend it, and in whose name both of you — but most urgently you, today — must be reconciled to God before you can be reconciled to each other.

I'm going to speak plainly, because you're asking for plainness, and the Westminster Standards do too.

You're asking the right question of the right man: "What do I owe?" The Standards answer it in the same place you already suspect — the Confession on repentance, the 8th and 9th commandments, and the chapter on oaths. Let me take your objections in order, then give you the sequence.

---

### On T2 — "God's forgiven me, can't I file it under that?"

No. And this is the dangerous one, so I want to be precise.

WCF 15.3 is explicit: *"Although repentance be not to be rested in, as any satisfaction for sin, or any cause of the pardon thereof, which is the act of God's free grace in Christ; yet it is of such necessity to all sinners, that none may expect pardon without it."* Forgiveness removes the *penal* guilt — the eternal weight — but it does not cancel the *fruits* of repentance. WCF 15.5 names the fruit: *"endeavoring to walk in obedience to all the commandments of God."*

The Larger Catechism is even sharper when read in context of the Lord's Supper. The communicant preparing to receive is to be found *"humbling themselves for sin, and resolving against it; the examining of themselves... the renewing of their covenant with God, and of their vows to him... and endeavoring to the uttermost to recover and make restitution for wrongs done"* (WLC 173). You have been taking the bread and the cup — rightly feeling the burden — but not walking the path the Standards lay out for the very man who feels that burden.

The Catechism on the 9th commandment (Q145) lists *perjury* and *"concealing the truth, the guiltiness of our own sins... when called to witness for the truth"* together. Your sin isn't a one-time wrong you can relegate to a clean ledger. It is an ongoing deception so long as the record stands uncorrected and the people harmed remain deceived. The doctrine of forgiveness doesn't let you keep them deceived in peace.

As for the "boss's sin really, I was practically a kid" — the Standards don't let you delegate moral agency. WCF 6 makes every man a free, responsible actor. Coached into sin is still sin. Twenty-six is fully accountable. You're right that your boss bears his own guilt before God — but that judgment is his, not yours to use as a defense.

This objection fails. The next one is harder.

---

### On T3 — "Surely God doesn't require me to blow up my family"

WCF 2.2: *"God requireth of every man... faith and obedience... such... as he requireth, not impossible."* He does not command what you cannot do. And the Catechism, on the 8th commandment, gives a careful framework in the "rule of equity" — the Westminster Standards treat restitution as a real duty, but they are not naïve about the limits of a man's estate.

So you are not being asked to do the impossible. You are being asked to do the *possible*. Several things follow:

1. **The doctrine of impossibility cuts both ways.** You are not required to do what is beyond your power — including paying sums beyond your means in a manner that abandons your own dependents, who are also entrusted to your care. The Standards do not pit your children against your neighbors in a zero-sum contest. They give you a third path: the rule of equity, which measures what is feasible and faithful together.
2. **The doctrine of necessity does not license delay.** Difficulty, scandal, and cost are not the same thing as impossibility. The Standards are plain that "shall not perish, but have everlasting life" is a sufficient motive, and they reject the idea that hardship erases duty.
3. **You don't get to be your own risk assessor.** The practical judgment of "what is the right, feasible, faithful path" must be made under the counsel of your pastor and a Christian attorney — not alone at 3 a.m., where fear is doing the discerning.

There is a workable path that does not involve "legal suicide." But you don't get to pre-empt it by deciding that the cost is too high. You get to walk through it soberly with the right advisors at your side.

---

### On T4 — "Anonymous charity to fire victims, debt paid"

This is the most seductive one because it has the *shape* of restitution without the *substance* of it. The Standards are clear about why it fails.

**WLC 141** on the 8th commandment names among required duties: *"restoring what we have taken from any, by unrighteous means."* The duty is to *them*, not to *their class*. Restitution is named to the *person* wronged. A gift to a charity, however good, is charity; it is not restitution. The two are different works.

Second — and this is the deeper problem — the harm you did is not only financial. The deposition stands. The record lies. The opposing party's case was weaker than it ought to have been because of your oath. The family *believes* the record is true, and they have built their understanding of the case on that lie. An anonymous cheque does not correct that. The Standards on the 9th commandment don't just require paying for harm; they require *"the maintaining and promoting of truth between man and man"* (WLC 144). The lie must end. The truth must be told.

So no — that is not a substitute. It may be one part of what you owe (a generous, concrete care for the specific family, if they will accept it and where it is right), but it is not the whole, and it is not the chief.

The Standards demand: tell the truth, restore what is reasonably computable as loss, and do it to the persons harmed, by the rule of equity, in the most faithful manner available.

---

### T5 — The actual sequence

This is the part where the Standards point in a direction, and Christian counsel walks you down it. I will give you the order, then the people in the room.

**Step 0 — Today, before anything public: confide, do not broadcast.** Tell your wife. Not because she gives permission, but because (a) the lie was committed alone and the repentance must not be, and (b) what you are about to do affects her and the children materially; she must not be a passive bystander. The 9th commandment's demand for integrity cannot coexist with managing her in a quiet lie by omission. (See also the marriage duties in the Standards — you are one flesh; the decision is hers to share in.)

**Step 1 — Spiritual counsel within the week.** Go to your pastor, or to two or three elders if your pastor is not the right person. WCF 30 and the Directory for Church Government treat grave, hidden-to-the-world sins as a matter for the elders' care. Do not try to be your own counselor here. The 3 a.m. loop is itself evidence that the work is too heavy for your study lamp.

Bring the facts you know: the deposition, what you swore to, what was true, the names of the parties, your boss, the lawyers, the settlement amount, and what you understand of the present circumstances of the family. Be specific. The Standards require an honest, searching inquiry into the sin (WCF 15.4) — vague guilt is the enemy of real repentance.

**Step 2 — Legal counsel, with a Christian lawyer, before you do anything visible.** The standards of the bar require a lawyer to do his duty by you, and a Christian one will also care for your conscience. You need answers to specific questions, and the answers change the path:

- Is perjury or perjury-related exposure still legally live, or has the statute of limitations run? (Most jurisdictions run a 3–5 year clock on perjury; many run 6–7 on fraud-based civil claims. I am not your lawyer, and I do not know your jurisdiction. Your lawyer does.)
- What is the mechanism to correct a deposition of that age in your jurisdiction? (Affidavit of correction; reopening the matter; contacting counsel of record; voluntary disclosure to the court.)
- How would a corrected testimony interact with the long-final settlement? Can the settlement be revisited by mutual consent, or has the legal question gone to rest? Be prepared for the answer "no, legally it cannot be undone" — which is not the same as "morally nothing is owed."
- If the SOL has run, what is the realistic criminal exposure? Often very low for a cooperative, self-disclosing party on a 9-year-old civil case. Often zero.
- If there is exposure, how does a voluntary, cooperative correction affect the risk profile? Almost always it reduces it; a prosecutor's enthusiasm for prosecuting a man who came forward of his own accord, on a 9-year-old matter that the original plaintiff never appealed, is low.

Do not act on this with one email, then stop. The legal architecture must be mapped before the moral step is taken.

**Step 3 — Pastoral and elder review of the legal path.** Bring the lawyer's letter back to the elders. The Standards expect joint discernment where the consequences are grave. The elders are to confirm, with the lawyer's input, that the path you are about to take is the one of obedience and not the one of self-punishment masquerading as faith.

**Step 4 — Private disclosure to the family, where possible.** The Standards are not squeamish about a Christian owning the worst of his sin before the persons he wronged. WLC 144 calls for *"appearing and standing for the truth."* In most cases, this means a face-to-face meeting with the family, lawyer present, with the elders' support. You tell them:

- That you have been living with a lie.
- Specifically, that your deposition testimony under oath was false on the matter of the sprinkler inspection.
- That you understand your false testimony contributed to a weaker case against your former employer.
- That you are here to tell the truth now and to ask what restitution is owed.
- That you have come forward, with counsel, of your own accord, and are willing to participate in correcting the legal record.

You do not lead with the boss, you do not lead with your age, you do not lead with the cost to you. You lead with the truth they were denied. *Then* the cost and the path are discussed.

**Step 5 — Correcting the legal record.** Through your lawyer, a sworn corrective statement or affidavit; if the original proceeding can be revisited, a stipulation to do so; otherwise, the truth communicated to the court of record. The deposition was sworn; the correction is sworn. (The Standards on oaths, WCF 22, bind you symmetrically — your oath binds you to truth both when you made it and now to undo your untruth.)

**Step 6 — Material restitution by the rule of equity.** This is the part that requires the elders' and the lawyer's judgment, not yours alone. The Standards expect reasonable, honest, painful-but-possible restitution, calibrated to the actual loss and the actual means of the wrongdoer. It is not punitive impoverishment; it is not a token. It is *"to the uttermost to recover and make restitution"* in the language of WLC 173.

**Step 7 — Public confession in your own church.** Once the legal exposure is past, the private parties have been told, the record is corrected, the elders are satisfied — the Standards expect a confession commensurate with how the sin was committed. This was a public, judicially-occasioned sin, hidden behind a settlement. Your church must know. The Confession on church discipline (WCF 30) treats such cases; the path is grave but the destination is restored communion. (You will not be asked to wear a sign; the WCF gives the church, not the crowd, the authority and the duty.)

**Step 8 — Sustained repentance.** This is not a single weekend. WCF 13 on sanctification: mortification of the flesh and the lusts thereof is the work of a lifetime. You will, by grace, be tempted to minimize, reframe, and forget. Do the visible disciplines that will make this hard for you to do: regular confession to your wife, regular check-ins with your pastor, ongoing giving to the specific family if they will accept it, sustained work in the ordinary means of grace.
