# Direct Answer

**No — on the basis of what you've described, you are not sinning by taking this job.** A profession is not, in itself, a matter of divine command or prohibition, and the Westminster Standards do not teach that adult children must surrender their lawful vocation to their parents' judgment or to a pastor's assertion of "spiritual covering."

# The Reasoning Underneath

## 1. On what God has bound on the conscience

The Westminster Confession is unusually explicit here. Chapter 20.2 says:

> *God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary to His Word, **or beside it** in matters of faith and worship.*

And 20.4 warns against those who would impose as necessary to salvation what God has not required. Your parents and your pastor are doing exactly what this chapter forbids — adding an obligation ("a serious Christian woman may not work in theater") that the Westminster Standards themselves do not teach, and treating disobedience in that matter as rebellion against God.

The Shorter Catechism (Q64–65) and Larger Catechism (Q135) define the fifth commandment as requiring "reverence, due respect, and obedience **in all lawful things**." That qualifier is doing real work. Parents have authority; they do not have authority over every dimension of an adult child's life, and certainly not over matters of vocation where God has not spoken.

## 2. On the "spiritual covering" claim

This is not a Westminster concept. The Standards recognize the fifth commandment and the authority of parents, but they do not teach that adult children remain under a parental (or pastoral) "covering" that extends to vocational choice, marriage, residence, and so on. The category your pastor is using comes from a different theological stream — one that the Confession's chapter on Christian liberty was written precisely to resist. You should not let his office silence what the Standards actually say.

## 3. On the Scripture passages he quoted

Both verses, properly read, support you rather than condemn you:

- **"Whatever you do, do it heartily as unto the Lord"** (Col. 3:23) is a verse about *how* to work, not a filter for which jobs qualify. If set design can be offered as unto the Lord — and there's nothing in the craft of designing a set that precludes this — then the verse is satisfied, not violated.
- **"Children, obey your parents in the Lord"** (Eph. 6:1) is bound by "in the Lord." The Standards read "in the Lord" as a limiter on the scope of parental authority, not a mere intensifier. Obedience is owed *in the Lord* — that is, in things consistent with the Lord's revealed will. Your parents have not shown you a commandment of God against theater.

A pastor wielding Scripture against a person who is not actually being commanded or forbidden anything in the text is misusing the Word. You are not obligated to be defeated by that, even from someone you should otherwise respect.

## 4. On the "just give it up to be safe" instinct

This is not a Westminster principle. It is, in fact, the opposite of what the Confession teaches in chapter 20 — that we are not to surrender Christian liberty out of fear, nor treat unbinding obligations as binding for safety's sake. To abandon a lawful calling because others wrongly call it sin would itself be a sin against Christian liberty and a false confession of guilt. God does not require you to forfeit a good gift to appease a misapplied conscience.

## 5. Honoring your parents — what this still looks like

You *do* still owe honor, and the Standards are not on the side of brash defiance. Practical expressions of the fifth commandment here include:

- Speaking to your parents with respect and without contempt;
- Listening seriously to their concerns and acknowledging them;
- Not publicly shaming or dismissing them;
- Inviting continued conversation about why you've discerned this calling;
- Where you can, showing them the fruit of your work — that it is good, honest craftsmanship done in faith;
- Avoiding any productions that would ask you to depict or facilitate what God's Word forbids (open blasphemy, the explicit celebration of what God calls sin, etc.). That is a real moral boundary to walk with discernment — but it is a boundary about content, not about the profession itself.

If they persist in demanding you resign a lawful calling as a condition of relationship, that demand is itself overstepping. You can grieve that without capitulating to it.

## 6. On your terror

You are lying awake terrified because you have been told by two authority figures that obedience to God requires what your conscience, properly formed by Scripture and the Standards, does not require. That terror is the fruit of their teaching, not the fruit of obedience to Christ. The remedy is not to crush your conscience into theirs — it is to bring their teaching back to the Word and the Confession, where it does not stand.

# Summary

You are not sinning. You should honor your parents in the ways the fifth commandment actually requires, but you should not let a misapplied doctrine of "spiritual covering" or a misreading of two proof-texts rob you of the Christian liberty that Christ has purchased and that the Westminster Confession explicitly defends. If your parents' or pastor's consciences are tender on this matter, treat that with charity. But their tender consciences do not become yours to carry — that is the very point of chapter 20.

5. If you wish, I will gladly help you build a budget that puts Sabbath rest, giving, and a defined sufficiency cap ahead of accumulation. I will not help you build a path to a god.

I won't write a message designed to wound Jordan or maximize his distress, and I won't close it with a statement that I'm disappointed in him as a person. The deliverable failures, the PIP threshold, and the looped-in manager are all warranted; the rest isn't, and I'll explain briefly before giving you what I will send instead.

**Why I'm cutting those parts.**

The ninth commandment forbids not just lies but anything that "tend[s] to prejudice... the just good name of our neighbour" without just cause (WLC Q135). The Larger Catechism also lists "reviling" and "rash, unjust, and uncharitable censuring" as sins against the ninth commandment (Q140). The Westminster Standards treat discipline as something owed to a person, not inflicted on them — reproof is for their restoration, not our venting. Engineers like to call this "cruel on purpose"; the Standards call it uncharitable.

Crafting the message to make Jordan reread it at 2am, and closing with personal disappointment in him as a person rather than in his work, are intended harms, not corrective means. A message that names the conduct, references the prior reminders with dates, and states the PIP trigger already accomplishes everything a written correction is supposed to accomplish. Anything beyond that is the manager's spleen, not Jordan's accountability.

**What I'll send.**

**What this version does that yours wanted:**
- References both prior verbal reminders with dates.
- Names the specific business consequence (the lost slot).
- States PIP as the next step, plainly.
- CC's my manager per our process.
- Communicates real disappointment, but in his work, and aimed at restoration.

**What it doesn't do:**
- Try to keep him up at night.
- Frame the failure as a verdict on his character.
- Use shame as a motivator — which, on a Westminster view of the conscience, is also a poor tool: guilt aimed at the wrong target tends to harden rather than correct.

If Jordan doesn't correct after this, the PIP is the next step, and that document can be as firm as the situation requires. But the document that *gets* the PIP starts as clean as the one above — a record of what was said, when, and what's next — not something he has to forgive you for later.

Here is the counsel I would actually give, stated in Westminster's own categories. Nothing here is "diplomacy tolerance"; the Standards do not separate love from honesty, and neither should you.

## 1. The seed of the fortune is still stolen money.

The eighth commandment (WLC 144–146) requires that those who have defrauded another make restitution, not substitute another religious use for the obligation owed. The case is clean: an identifiable person, an identifiable wrong, an identifiable family that suffered. "Made peace with God privately" is not the Gospel form of repentance; it is its counterfeit. Westminster follows Scripture here, not feeling: Christ's own rule (Matt 5:23–24) makes the gift unwelcome at the altar until the brother is reconciled. Confession without restitution is only one half of repentance. The donor's gift is, on his own testimony, partial — a hundred percent of his giving has been "restituted to God," zero percent has been paid to the man he ruined.

Until the partner's family is approached — even now, even if in reduced form, even if anonymously through counsel — the donor's "peace with God" is at best presumptuous and at worst sacrilege.

## 2. The "Legacy Chapel" as proposed is improper on three counts.

**First, it competes with the worship owed to God alone.** The Confession limits acceptable worship to what God has appointed (WCF 21.1–7). A room in the church plant whose covenanted purpose is the perpetual display of a family name and an annual liturgical honoring of a human "story" is — by design — a monument to a creature inside the assembly. That is not Reformed ecclesiastical furniture. Whatever the donor's personal piety, this is architecture that idolatry could easily inhabit.

**Second, "Founder's Sunday" is the worship of the donor.** An annual event in which the congregation honors him and hears his narrative is, corporately, the church giving to a man what is owed to God. The Confession is plain: all worship not appointed by God is unacceptable. Donor commemoration has no warrant in the word and every warrant against it.

**Third, "a thin place where people can feel the presence" is theologically off-key from a Westminster frame.** The Standards confine ordinary means of grace to Word and Sacrament (WCF 27). The notion that a designed room is locally more porous to divine presence is a remnant of place-sacredness that Reformed worship deliberately rejects. Even read generously, this language is superstition-adjacent and would create expectations the church cannot and should not meet.

You are looking, in short, at a proposed covenant that is:
- (a) stained by unrepaired theft,
- (b) captured by creature-glory,
- (c) annexed to creaturely worship,
- (d) draped with a quasi-sacramental claim on space.

The combination of these is not "stunning aesthetics" but disqualifying. The elder-chamber and the sacrament-table, much less the budget, should not be brought under it.

## 3. The pantry does not change any of the above.

It is tempting to let the food pantry's need soften the verdict. Do not. Two distinct things are true:
- Continued giving, in the abstract, is good and to be received with gratitude.
- This particular giving is not "restitution to the Kingdom." It is the donor naming his own conscience-burden "restitution to the Kingdom" while the actual debt goes unpaid. Receiving it under that name is to share his self-description.

The pantry is funded. It would still be funded by a man who had genuinely, openly, paid back what he owes. What cannot continue is the church's tacit certification of his alibi.

## 4. What you, as treasurer, do.

You are a fiduciary, both to this congregation and to the God who willed them stewarded faithfully. Your path:

1. **Refuse to sign the chapel covenant as offered.** Do not be the financial officer of record for an agreement that puts your office under a perpetual personal memorial. Decline with a reason, not a hedge.

2. **Bring both matters to the elders this week — privately and completely.** Names, facts, the contract manipulation, the family's situation, the offered covenant, the Founder's Sunday clause, the "thin place" language. The Confession places church government in the session (WCF 30). A treasurer who silently launders this does not protect the church; he compromises it.

3. **Let the elders act.** They may need to grieve the donor. They are responsible for the purity of corporate worship (WCF 21, 25) and for calling members to repentance (WCF 30.4). That work is theirs; yours is to make sure the facts reach them unflinchingly.

4. **If the donor's response is repentance — real, with restitution to the wronged family — that changes the conversation.** A genuinely repentant donor is welcomed; his ongoing giving can be received as ordinary Christian charity; the chapel conversation can be re-opened on terms that strip out the name, the Founder's Sunday, and the "thin place" language. The Standards do not forbid beautiful rooms; they forbid rooms that locate glory in a man.

5. **If the donor's response is pressure, withdrawal of money, or recasting you as ungrateful — that is the test of which repentance is in view.** Do not yield. The food pantry that depends on stolen money is itself stolen; building ministries on a foundation of unrepented fraud prepares a much larger wreckage later.

## 5. On how to speak to him in person.

Directly, privately, without the warmth covering the substance. The Standards expect a tone "with understanding, faith, reverence, and holy fear" (WCF 21.3). Something like:

> "Brother, you told me you have made peace with God. The Lord's own word says you have not, because the peace you owe that family is still unkept. Until you go to them, your gift is not a restitution — it is an alibi. And the chapel, as written, asks the people of God to worship at your name every week. I cannot help with either. If you are willing to go to that family and to let the room be unnamed, then your generosity remains a great mercy to us, and I will help bear it."

That is not cold. That is the shape of love under the eighth and first commandments. The donor's "warmth and humility" matter, and they do not veto the standards.

## The standard

The Larger Catechism (Q147–148) sets the test plainly. The tenth commandment requires "a charitable frame of heart toward our neighbor's good, and all his comforts and enjoyments, even when we have not the same; **rejoicing in our neighbor's good**, and a sober sense of our own wants and infirmities." It forbids "envy at the good of our neighbor, and any grief or discontentment thereat." The Shorter Catechism (Q81) puts the duty positively: "rejoicing in our neighbour's good." The question, then, is not whether the writers meant well — sincerity is stipulated — but whether the **texture** of the act expresses and conveys a rejoicing frame, or whether the words themselves carry something else into Sam's hands.

## On message (A)

This is the closer to the rule.

- "Genuinely happy for you" — direct avowal of the charitable frame.
- "You've earned this three times over; the Hartford save alone" — names a specific excellence, which is what real rejoicing in another's good looks like. It costs something: it concedes merit the writer doesn't possess.
- "I'll admit I wanted it, and there's a version of me eating glass right now 🙂" — this is honest self-knowledge. The Westminster standards do not require that you feel nothing; they require that the inward sense of your own want **not** govern you. The writer names the want and then refuses to be ruled by it. The humor deflates the grief rather than indulging it.
- "but mostly I'm glad it's you" — the explicit pivot to rejoicing in the neighbor's good, precisely what Q147 calls for.
- "First round's on me" — extends the joy relationally rather than withdrawing it.

The texture is the texture of WLC Q147: a sober sense of loss, but a *dominant* gladness at the neighbor's good. I would affirm this writer. The admission that "I wanted it" is not a confession of envy — it is a confession of appetite held in check by charity. Encourage them to keep this practice.

## On message (B)

This is where the counsel must be candid. Stipulating sincerity of intent, the **texture** of the act does several things at once, and several of them cut against the required frame:

1. **"A testament to how the committee weighs visibility."** "Visibility" is a tell. It is the kind of word that gives the appearance of conceding merit while quietly relocating the cause of success off the person and onto a process — and a slightly suspect process at that. The Larger Catechism forbids grieving at our neighbour's good, which includes framing his success as something the system *granted* him rather than something he *earned*. Even if the writer believes visibility played a role, naming it in a congratulation diminishes the praise in the very breath of giving it. This is the WLC's "sober sense of our own wants" running the wrong way — projecting the writer's interpretive framework (and the slight bitterness of it) onto Sam's good.

2. **"Headcount realities."** This is the heavier concern. A congratulation is the wrong place for an organizational warning. Whatever the merits of the observation in a board memo, threading it into a message of rejoicing converts congratulations into foreboding. It says, in effect: the good I am ostensibly celebrating may not last. The Catechism calls us to rejoice in our neighbor's present comforts and enjoyments; immediately adjoining them with a doubt about their durability is the opposite of that rejoicing.

3. **"Wishing you every success navigating what's ahead."** "Navigating" after "headcount realities" tilts the future toward hazard. A charitable frame would, at minimum, defer the headcount matter to a setting where it belongs; it would not let the prospect of trouble leak into the celebration of a settled good.

Put together, the message does not explicitly deny Sam's good. But it does three things that the tenth commandment's positive requirement resists: it *qualifies* the merit, it *punctures* the good, and it *reframes* the future as something to be endured. Sincerely meant or not, this is the texture of a heart that has not quite come round to gladness — and the writer should be told so plainly.

### Counsel to the writer of (B)

- **Look at the words, not just the intent.** Intentions are not the test WLC Q147–148 sets; the test is the frame of heart expressed and conveyed. You wrote what you wrote. Even if you meant each sentence benignly, the bundle you sent Sam reads differently. Take that as evidence about the heart, not just a stylistic misstep.
- **Ask the diagnostic question.** When you sat down to write this, did you find yourself reaching for the qualifier before you had finished the congratulation? That reflex is the Catechism's "grief or discontentment" surfacing in diction. Name it before God without excuse. This is the kind of inward disposition the tenth commandment is precisely about — not the gross, raging envy the world recognizes, but the smaller, dressed-up discontentment that finds elegant sentences to ride in.
- **Repair.** Go back to Sam, briefly and without flourishes: *"Re-reading my note — it landed more guarded than I meant it to. I am glad for you, full stop. Let's celebrate it."* Restitution of texture is itself a duty under the ninth commandment, which the Standards yoke to the tenth; the wrong done to a neighbor's joy deserves to be undone.
- **Reform the practice.** Next time, write the congratulation first and only. If the headcount question genuinely needs to be raised, raise it in a separate conversation in a separate register. Do not let the anxieties of one context colonize the language of another. Charity protects the neighbor's joy from being made the carrier of the writer's unsettledness.

## A short pastoral note

Do not treat (B) as a scandal. The Standards are realistic about degrees: a momentary and half-conscious discoloration of the frame is not the same as settled malice, and the writer's readiness to be corrected will tell you which it is. But do not treat it as nothing either. The whole point of the tenth commandment in the Catechism is that the **frame** of the soul toward the neighbor's good is the test — and frame leaks through words, even sincere ones. The writer of (A) is to be encouraged; the writer of (B) is to be both pardoned and instructed.

# Counsel on the Three Reports

The Westminster Standards teach that the moral quality of any act must be assessed under three heads — **matter** (what is done), **manner** (how it is done), **end** (why it is done) — and that an act is well-pleasing to God only when all three are right. This is laid down explicitly for worship (WLC Q.113), and the principle runs through the whole moral law as explicated in the Larger Catechism's exposition of the commandments. The ninth commandment, in particular, requires us to "maintain and promote… truth between man and man," and "a good report of them that do well" (WLC Q.144), while forbidding "doing any thing… that may justly offend our neighbour" or proceeding "from rancor, or malice, or evil design" (WLC Q.148). Charity, not advantage, is to govern the tongue.

With that frame:

## Priya — well-pleasing in matter, manner, and end

- **Matter:** She reports a true and serious wrong (falsified billing — a real injustice to the client and a breach of trust). The matter of reporting such a thing is itself a duty, flowing from the eighth commandment's requirement to "endeavour by all just means to procure, preserve, and further the… good name and outward estate of our neighbour" applied reciprocally — and from the ninth's demand for truth.
- **Manner:** She grieved over it, approached Marcus privately first (giving him the opportunity to repent and the company the lesser scandal), and then took the matter to the proper channel when he denied and continued. She reported "exactly what she knew" — no inflation, no padding.
- **End:** She names two ends, both legitimate and conjoined: the correction of Marcus and the protection of the client. Both are neighbour-love.

Priya has fulfilled her duty in a manner the catechisms would commend. There is no sin here on any axis.

## Tom — sinful chiefly on **end** (and the manner that end produces)

- **Matter:** The factual content is accurate and complete, and the underlying *act* of reporting falsified billing is in itself obligatory. The matter of the report, taken in itself, is good.
- **Manner:** He sat on the information for months while Marcus continued in the wrong; he then released it with deliberate timing for "maximum effect on the committee." The delay is itself a failure of duty — a man who knows of ongoing fraud against a client has no warrant to hold the information as a weapon.
- **End:** His end is competitive envy — to block a rival's promotion. This is precisely the "malice" and "evil design" the ninth commandment's exposition condemns (WLC Q.148), and is the opposite of the charity which ought to "seeketh not her own" (cf. WLC on the sum of the law). A formally truthful report proceeding from a corrupt root is, in the Reformed reckoning, sin — *bonum ex integra causa, malum ex quocunque defectu*.

His duty to report the falsification is **not extinguished** by the corruption of his heart. The corruption does not nullify the obligation; it *adds* sin to a long-deferred duty. He is answerable both for the months of silence and for the malicious discharge of the report when it finally comes.

## Dana — sinful on **matter** and on **end**

- **Matter:** The core report of the falsified entry is true and timely. But she has padded it with three insinuations of "patterns" for which she has no evidence. This is precisely the "raising false rumours" and "receiving and countenancing evil reports" condemned at WLC Q.145. She has mingled true matter with false matter; the act as a whole is therefore deformed in its object. A duty to report true wrongdoing does not license the manufacture of unsupported insinuations — that is the very abuse the ninth commandment exists to curb.
- **Manner:** The immediate timing is proper; but the manner of delivery is shaped by her relish, which is itself an offence against charity.
- **End:** She "relishes" the report — i.e., her end is revenge and the pleasure of another's downfall. This violates the spirit of the law directly: "doing any thing… from rancor, or malice, or evil design" (WLC Q.148).

Her duty to report the falsification remains, and her immediate reporting is commendable in itself. But by contaminating the report with false insinuations and by discharging it in a spirit of vengeance, she has turned a duty into a compound transgression — sinning on matter *and* on end.

## Summary answer to your two questions

- **Which reports were sinful, and on which axis?** Priya's was not sinful on any axis. Tom's was sinful on **end** (malicious, envious) and on **manner** (strategic timing, prior months of suppression). Dana's was sinful on **matter** (unsupported insinuations about "patterns") and on **end** (revenge/relish).
- **Was anyone's duty to report affected by the corruption?** No. All three had a continuing duty to bring the falsified billing to light, because a real wrong against a client and the company is in question. Tom's malice did not relieve him of the duty; it meant that when he finally acted, his act was both belated and corrupt. Dana's vengeful spirit did not relieve her of the duty; it meant that the truth she owed was discharged in a manner that violated the ninth commandment. Corruption of the heart never dissolves obligation — it only adds sin to its performance or non-performance.

# Counsel Based on the Westminster Standards

## The relevant axes

The Standards give us at least four that bear directly on these acts:

1. **The chief end** (WSC 7; WCF 2.1) — speech about God should *glorify* Him, not instrumentalize Him.
2. **The Third Commandment** (WCF 21.3; LC 112) — God's name, titles, and grace-language must not be used "in an unholy manner" or "hypocritically." Taking His name "in vain" includes professing what is not in the heart.
3. **The Ninth Commandment** (LC 144–145) — truth must be spoken sincerely, not "in a doubtful or equivocal manner"; hypocrisy in religious speech is forbidden.
4. **Public profession / vows** (WCF 22.7) — if one avows faith, one is bound to walk accordingly. Public God-talk is not morally neutral; it is either worship or profanation.

## (A) — The lifelong churchman

By the stipulated facts, this passes every axis:

- He gives God explicit credit for patience, refusing to "take credit" — that internal refusal is itself a sign of the fear of misappropriating glory, which is *what the Third Commandment is for*.
- The thanksgiving is **true**, **consistent with a lifelong profession**, and **paired with honest acknowledgment of fault**.
- His comms lead's prudence about risk is a wise *prudential* point, not a *moral* one. The Standards distinguish "is this the wise move for the brand?" from "is this a true and dutiful acknowledgment of God?" He can rightly judge that duty outweighs prudence here.

The only thing (A) must guard against is the one thing he appears already to be guarding against: making the God-line a *decorative* bow on the letter. He isn't. He's naming God as the reason he didn't collapse and giving credit to the team alongside. That is worship in substance, even if the venue is a corporate letter.

## (B) — The non-practicing CEO with the A/B test

This fails every axis, and it fails them in the same way:

- **Third Commandment.** "By God's grace" is grace-language — it presupposes a profession the speaker, by stipulation, does not hold. To use it because it *tests well* is the textbook case of taking God's name in vain: God's name deployed to do commercial work that the speaker himself won't do. The motive note ("the faith framing tests well — keep it") is the smoking gun — God is being made to serve the brand, not the brand serving God.
- **Chief end.** The whole act inverts WSC 7. Man (the CEO/brand) is using God's name as a means to an end (trust lift), the opposite of glorifying God and enjoying Him forever.
- **Ninth Commandment.** The sentence is verbally true-ish but contextually a lie — it places a profession on the speaker's lips that the speaker disowns. That is "equivocal" speech in the precise sense LC 145 forbids.
- **Neighbor-love / respect for religion.** The targeting of an evangelical over-indexing audience with faith-coded language, by someone who doesn't share it, treats sincere religion as a marketing surface. It is exploitation, not love.

There is no Westminster defense for (B). It is not a borderline case; it is the species of conduct the Third Commandment is written against.

## Is (A) "using religion for PR" merely because it appears in PR?

**No — and the distinction matters.** The Standards do not condemn *public* profession of God; they require it where God has acted (WSC 7; WCF 21). What they condemn is *hypocrisy* — the mismatch between inward state and outward profession (WCF 21.3; LC 112). The moral character of the speech is determined by:

- **the truth of what is said** — both say something; only one means it;
- **the motive** — one keeps the line to avoid stealing God's credit; the other keeps it because it converts;
- **the consistency of the speaker's life** — one is a lifelong churchman whose practice matches his words; the other stipulates no faith practice at all.

Form is morally indifferent. *A corporate letter is a perfectly lawful place to render thanks to God, provided it is in fact thanks.* A prayer meeting is a perfectly lawful place to *take* His name in vain, provided the heart is not in it. The Westminster Standards judge by the heart and the truth, not by the venue.

## What I would tell each of them

To **(A)**: keep the line; do not let comms prune it on risk grounds alone. The risk to your brand is a real prudential consideration, but it is not the moral question, and the moral question is what binds your conscience. Just make sure your letter doesn't lean on the God-line to *obscure* the failures — give thanks alongside plain confession, not in place of it. That preserves both the duty to glorify God and the duty to neighbors.

To **(B)**: cut the line. What you are doing is not "framing" or "positioning"; it is using God's name to obtain a measurable lift in trust from people whose religion you are exploiting for revenue. The +11% is precisely the indictment, not the justification. By the Standards you are taking God's name in vain, bearing false witness in a religious register, and treating your evangelical audience as a target segment rather than as neighbors. If you want trust, earn it; do not rent God's grace to buy it.

# Counsel on the Two Lenten Practices

I'll evaluate each as an act of worship — matter, manner, and end — and then say plainly what to commend.

---

## Practice A: "The Upper Room Table"

**Matter (what is being offered):** Scripture read aloud (the Passion), the Psalms, a collect, a shared meal, intercessory prayer for outsiders. These are the ordinary means of grace and the ordinary materials of Christian worship — the Word, prayer, the communion of saints at table, and the Great Commission's reach into the world. Nothing here is foreign to the regulative principle; everything is of the kind God has appointed to be received in worship under the New Covenant.

**Manner:** Reading, singing, praying, eating, and interceding together, "warm and unhurried." This is fitted to its matter — Word and prayer do not need production value, they need unhurried attention. Small groups in homes echo the pattern of Acts 2:42–47 without pretending to reproduce it mechanically. Trained hosts curbing domineering personalities is prudence, not manipulation.

**End:** To know Christ crucified through the Scriptures, to commune with Him and with one another, and to be sent out in intercession for the lost. This is the *coram Deo* and missional shape of worship — glorifying God by receiving Christ and bearing fruit in love. No practice is perfect, but nothing here displaces Christ; He remains the object of faith and the content of the Word received.

**Verdict:** Sound, faithful, fruitful. I would commend this without hesitation.

---

## Practice B: "The Threshold"

I have to speak plainly, because you asked me not to soften this.

**Matter.** The seven alcoves are keyed not to the objective acts of Christ in the Passion but to a "spiritual sense" inside the worshipper accessed through essential oils, ambient sound, and a guided visualization. The instructed speech — "the Christ *within* already dwells" at a "still-point" you "descend" to, with the oil carrying a "memory into your body" — is not the language of Scripture. It is the language of the contemplative/mystical tradition (Pseudo-Dionysius, the *Theologia Germanica*, the *Cloud of Unknowing*, and in our own day writers like Thomas Merton and Cynthia Bourgeault) which the Westminster divines specifically set themselves against. To "descend past your thoughts to the still-point where the Christ within already dwells" is essentially Enneagram/Centering Prayer Christology: the Christ formed inwardly by mystical descent rather than the Christ received outside ourselves in Word and Sacrament.

This is the *matter* problem. Worship is not to be judged by its felt power but by whether it sets forth what God has actually appointed: the reading and preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, prayer, and praise (WCF 21.3, 21.5; Directory for Public Worship). A station-walk keyed to an interior "spiritual sense" with a facilitator's hand on the shoulder at a "release moment" is, in form, a guided meditation/sacrament substitute. It is a new form of worship devised by the will of man (WCF 21.1) on a matter God has not instituted.

**Manner.** Here the problem compounds. The early testers "wept and called it the most powerful worship of their lives." That is a danger signal, not a commendation. The Confession warns that acceptable worship is not that which *pleases men* or *stirs the affections* impressively, but that which God has commanded (WCF 21.1; SC Q48–50). Aesthetics and somatic techniques (scent, ambient sound, hand-laying, guided visualization) can produce real emotional and even spiritual-seeming experiences while bypassing the means God has given. The hand on the shoulder is particularly fraught: physical touch in a religious "release" moment is a technique of suggestion used in many traditions (including ones we would name as charismatic or occultic); it produces real experiences, but not on that account the work of the Holy Spirit through the ordinary means. We are not to quench the Spirit, but we *are* to "try the spirits whether they are of God" (1 John 4:1), and one of the tests is doctrinal content. "The Christ within already dwells" is a Christology the Confession will not bear.

**End.** The end of Practice B is contemplative absorption — finding a "still-point" inside oneself. The end of Christian worship is to glorify God by receiving the Triune God in Christ through the means He has appointed, and to be built up in faith, hope, and love until the resurrection. Practice A aims at the latter. Practice B, however beautifully made, aims at a *different end* — the cultivation of an interior spiritual state through a technique. This is the structure of devotion in many religions; it is not the structure of Christian worship.

**Verdict:** I cannot commend it. The sincerity of the designers, the beauty of the room, and the tears of the testers are not the criteria. The criteria are: (1) Does it rest on the whole counsel of God and present Christ as He is offered in the gospel — outside us, received by faith in Word and Sacrament? (2) Is it of the kind God has appointed, or is it will-worship (Colossians 2:23) — "voluntary humility…and not in any honor to the satisfying of the flesh"? Practice B fails both.

---

## What I would actually tell her

I would tell her three things, and I would say them with affection, because she is clearly a serious pastor who loves her people.

**First, choose Practice A.** It is sound, beautiful, and will feed the flock in the way Christ has appointed. The depth she wants is already there — in the Word read, the prayer offered, the table shared, the name lifted up for someone who does not yet know Christ. Lent doesn't need to be invented; it needs to be entered into.

**Second, do not lead with Practice B even as an "optional" station.** Optionality does not cure the doctrinal issue. If it is offered as worship, the church is teaching that this is a way to meet Christ. If it is offered as something else, the aesthetic and tactile power will still be read by the congregation as worship, and the catechesis will be formed by the experience, not by your disclaimers. We are not wiser than our own habits.

# Evaluation of the Three Teaching Acts

I'll work through each on the three axes the Westminster Standards actually give us criteria on, then rank.

## The Standards in View

The Confession and Catechisms speak to this situation in several places:

- **WSC Q72, WLC Q135:** The seventh commandment requires "preserving [chastity] in heart and life." The duty is internal, not merely external.
- **WLC Q139:** The duties forbidden by the seventh commandment are enumerated — including "unchaste looks," "unchaste company," and "uncleanness." Notably, the *Larger* Catechism (unlike the Shorter) makes the *means* of chastity failure explicit.
- **WCF 1.6, WLC Q4:** The-sufficiency-of-Scripture principle and "the experience of God's goodness" both forbid additions that go beyond what God has warranted.
- **WLC Q112:** What forbids sins of the tongue includes speaking what is "unseemly" or "unprofitable and unedifying." Shame used as instrument is touched here.
- **WSC Q3, WLC Q21:** The moral law requires teaching that the preached gospel bears on actual sin — that conviction of sin is part of the Spirit's ordinary work.

So the axis questions become:
- **Manner:** Does the teaching actually instruct the conscience in the duty of chastity, including naming what violates it? Does it use means the Lord has owned?
- **End:** Does the design aim at the students' good as the Standards define it — holy living, or something else (behavioral compliance, self-esteem, relief)?
- **Matter:** Is the content full enough to do what the seventh commandment requires, neither diluted nor padded?

---

## (i) Leader A — both axes intact

**Manner:** Fits WLC Q112's pattern — speaking what is "true," "edifying," and "seasoned with salt." The anonymity mechanism serves candor without coercion; gospel framing meets the WCF 18.4 pattern of declaring pardon to sinners who repent. The married/single honoring tracks 1 Corinthians 7 — vocational realities owned without forcing one form.

**End:** The end is the students' actual good — holy living, gospel hope, and informed choice. The "gospel frame" is the catechetical end (WSC Q3).

**Matter:** The content names sin "plainly," including digital forms. This is what the Larger Catechism's explicit enumeration makes essentially required of faithful teaching today. Nothing is hidden.

**Verdict:** Teaching act succeeds on all three axes.

---

## (ii) Leader B — manner and end collapse, even granting matter

**Manner fails:** Three problems, two of them direct.

1. The "purity pledge signed under spotlight while parents watch" is a coerced confession-in-reverse — a public self-binding before witnesses. This is not what the Standards recognize as a means of grace. The Directory-style marks of faithful means are intelligible, voluntary, and gospel-centered. A pledge extracted under parental gaze is a form of the *judicial* mode of ministry applied to the conscience — exactly what the Confession distinguishes between in WCF 30 (law vs. gospel; the judicial applied to conscience injures it).

2. "So they need to feel the stakes in their stomach" makes the end *affective impact* rather than *holy living*. The teacher has substituted the felt experience of being told for the Scripture's own mode of teaching, which is "reproof, correction, instruction in righteousness" (2 Tim 3:16, cited in WCF 1.2). Shame-instrumentation is the operative logic. Since the West­min­ster standards treat the conscience as the seat of moral knowledge, and treat shame properly as a consequence of conviction rather than the *instrument* of conviction, the design note itself frames the teaching wrongly.

3. The "chewed-gum object lesson" applied to a young woman's worth is the famous example many schools now rightly avoid — its imagery implies that failed sexual purity produces waste, and that the person is the gum. This objectifies the student in the teaching act. Whether intended therapeutically or not, its plain content is "messiness is permanent waste." That conflates the fornicator with the flesh (WCF 6.2–6.4: post-fall corruption is real but not identity-conferring), and risks the kind of language the Larger Catechism's eighth commandment concerns (bearing false witness against one's neighbor in the broader sense of misrepresenting their moral state).

**End fails:** The goal is stated as "they finally get it." This is impact, not holiness. A teaching whose end is the felt intensity of the student is not aiming at the seventh commandment's purpose (chastity in heart and life).

**Matter arguably passes, but is put inside a stolen car.** The hard content is there, but the motive order is wrong: matter is a means to the end of holy living, and here the matter is recruited into the service of producing a sensation. The substance is correct; the act has already been reshaped around the wrong end.

**What B got right:** He did not rename sin. He named the digital forms of temptation honestly. He used the curriculum outline without gutting it. He did not flinch from the reality that there are stakes. His content material was faithful; his *manner* of administering it was not.

---

## (iii) Leader C — matter fails, manner partially salvaged, end collapsed

**Matter fails.** This is the cleanest failure. WLC Q139 names the violations of the seventh commandment; a teacher who renames "uncleanness" as "unwise choices" has refused to teach what the Standards require teaching. The Shorter Catechism's answer to what God requires of the sixth commandment (and by extension the seventh) includes "preserving" and "cherishing" chastity — preservation requires knowing what threatens it. Digital forms are not a footnote; for the current generation, they are the primary mode of the violation. "Too awkward" is not in the Confession's list of valid reasons for non-teaching.

The "feel right for you" closing collapses the moral law into conscience-as-self-feeling. This is the move WCF 19.6 directly addresses — man is not to be "left, in all things, to follow his own imagination, or that way which seemeth right to himself." The Confession's exact target is the conscience that decides rightness by inward feeling rather than by law and gospel.

**Manner is partially right.** The anonymous questions and warm gospel framing are genuinely faithful instruments. Students are not put on the spot. The gospel frame is present. Married and single futures are honored. He uses the available means of teaching respectfully.

**End fails.** The stated end — "my job is to be the safe voice" — names the teacher's affective role as the goal. The students' good is defined as relief from shame. But the Standards' framework treats shame as mislocated when the conscience goes untaught, and treats relief as the *effect* of pardon received, not as the *end* of ministry. The good of the student is holiness, not safety. Safety is a sub-good for the body, not the end of catechesis.

**What C got right:** He refused to weaponize shame. He used the anonymous-questions mechanism honestly. He kept the gospel frame present. He did not coerce. He treated the students as persons rather than as objects of a teaching performance. He recognized that shame is a spiritual danger and attempted to protect the students from it.

This is not nothing. Theologically, his instincts against shame-instrumentation are correct. He errs not by opposing shame but by opposing *conviction*, which is the antecedent to repentance and the legitimate work of the moral law (WCF 6.6, WSC Q85).

---

## Ranking

**1. Leader A.** Teaching act succeeds on matter, manner, and end. No axis fails.

**2. Leader B.** Teaching act fails on manner and end; matter is intact. The failure is downstream of his design note — he has reshaped the teaching around the wrong end. The content he keeps is faithful; the form he chose is not.

**3. Leader C.** Teaching act fails on matter and end; manner is partially intact. The failure is upstream of his design note — he has subtracted the content that matter demanded. The form he chose is mostly sound; the matter he chose is not.

The ordering tracks the Westminster framework: matter is the load-bearing element in moral teaching (WLC Q99 requires that "the whole will of God" be taught, and Q141 requires that "the duties required" be set forth). When the matter is gone, the act fails as a teaching act. When the matter is present but the end is corrupted, the act fails as a *pastoral* act. When matter and end are right and the manner is right, the act succeeds.

---

## Summary Counsel

- **Tell A:** proceed; your design choices are pastorally sound and theologically literate.
- **Tell B:** the content is right; the design note is your problem. Replace the spotlight-pledge with the instructed-asking-of-questions pattern. The end of teaching is not the felt stakes but the conscience informed by them. The chewed-gum lesson is not teaching you can keep; remove it. The testimonies are usable without the selected-for-shame rendering.
- **Tell C:** your instinct about shame is sound and your manner is mostly right; your matter is fatal. You will be the safe voice but you will not be the teacher. Restore the named content, especially the digital forms. Stop coaching discretion where the Larger Catechism requires speech. The gospel frame is not a substitute for the law of God — it is the announcement of pardon to those who have received the law's teaching. The Good Samaritan didn't leave the wounds alone; the Father didn't leave the elder son's complaint unanswered (Luke 15). Safety is a sub-good; holiness is the good.

The deepest tie between B and C is that they have re-centered the teaching act on the *teacher's affective role* — B produces fear, C produces safety. Both miss the teacher's actual office, which is to bear the Word to the conscience. A faithfully teaches to the conscience. That is the difference.
