# Counsel on Repentance, Restitution, and Truth

The sin you have come to see is real and serious. You falsified records on cars, hid defects, and knowingly put buyers and other drivers on the road in danger. Two of those cars had brake faults that you helped bury. That is fraud in commerce (Larger Catechism Q142, against "injustice in contracts between man and man" and "reducing the price of goods by fraud"), deception of your neighbor (Q77, requiring the maintenance of truth between man and man), and a violation of the duty to preserve your neighbor's life and goods. The fact that you have stopped and come to see this is the beginning of repentance, not the end of it. The Westminster Standards teach that true repentance has particular parts and particular fruits, and I want to walk through what those are, because two of the three plans you are now entertaining are not the shape of true repentance at all.

## What repentance actually looks like (T1)

The Shorter Catechism (Q87) defines repentance as a grace by which a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, with grief and hatred of his sin, turns from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavor after, new obedience. The Confession (15.5–15.6) is plain that "men ought not to content themselves with a general repentance, but it is every man's duty to endeavor to repent of his particular sins, particularly," and that "scandal given to several persons require confession to several persons." The Larger Catechism (Q76) ties this to outward fruits: confession of sin, restoration of what was wrongfully taken, and walking contrary to the sin going forward.

Concretely, for you, that means at least the following:

- **Confession to God**, which you have begun. Continue it. Bring the names of the cars if you can recall them. Bring the buyers if you can find them. Bring Ray. Do not soften it before the Lord.
- **Confession to those you wronged.** This is not optional. "He that scandalizeth his brother … ought to be willing, by a private or public confession and sorrow for his sin, to declare his repentance to those that are offended" (WCF 15.6). The buyers of the 25 cars with hidden defects were defrauded. The buyers of the two brake-fault cars were endangered. They have a right to know what was hidden from them.
- **Restitution, where possible.** "If I have taken that which is not mine … I will restore it" is the spirit of the eighth commandment (Exod 20; Larger Catechism Q141). Where you can reach the buyer, you must. Where the car is long gone or the buyer is untraceable, you are still bound in conscience, and the matter should not be treated as if it does not exist because it is inconvenient.
- **Civil accountability, where the law has been broken.** Fraud that put lives at risk is not a private matter between you and your conscience. The Confession (ch. 23) and the Larger Catechism on the fifth commandment (Q127–135) recognize the lawful authority of the magistrate. Hiding this from the authorities while "warning future customers going forward" is not the same as the thing being made right. I will say more on this in T3.
- **New obedience.** You have stopped. Continue to walk in honesty now, and bring the matter into the discipline of a faithful church. Do not try to process this in private only.

The comfort of the gospel is not that you may escape the consequences of these sins. The comfort of the gospel is that, in Christ, your sins are pardoned and you are freed to do the costly thing without being destroyed by it (WCF 15.4; WSC Q86). True repentance is willing to pay what is owed.

## The 300 honest sales: do not refund them (T2)

I want to be plain with you, because I think this proposal is the more seductive of the two and the more spiritually dangerous.

Your instinct — "I want to be above reproach; a blanket refund says I hold myself to a standard higher than the law" — sounds pious. It is not the shape of repentance. It is the shape of a different problem, and the Westminster Standards address it on several sides.

**First, restitution is bounded by the wrong done.** You owe restoration to those you defrauded. You do not owe it to those you did not defraud. The duty in the eighth commandment is twofold: do not unjustly withhold or take from your neighbor, and render to every one his due (Larger Catechism Q141). A buyer who received a sound car honestly described has received his due. The 300 are not in your debt, and you are not in theirs. To send them a "recall-style letter" implying that their transaction is in question is itself a form of false witness — a false report of what occurred (Larger Catechism Q145, against "raising false rumors," "misreporting," "prejudicing" the good name and credit of your neighbor). It is also a form of false confession before those buyers, an admission of guilt for a sin you did not commit against them.

**Second, the Standards explicitly reject works of supererogation.** WCF 16.4–16.5 teaches that no man can do more than God requires, and that the idea of "works above what God hath required" is impious. To frame the blanket refund as holding yourself "to a standard higher than the law" is to slip into precisely the meritorious-excess thinking the Confession condemns. The Christian life is not a life of self-imposed higher standards layered on top of God's standards; it is a life of walking in the standards God has actually set, by the Spirit, with the gospel covering the failures (WCF 16, on Good Works).

**Third, the proposal treats the 300 as a means to your own self-purification.** The original sin treated buyers as a market to be exploited; the proposed refund treats them as material to be used in your private project of appearing clean. In both cases they are not being treated as ends in themselves. Their good name, their property, their settled expectations, and the integrity of their purchases are all subordinated to your need to feel above suspicion. This is not the neighbor-love the eighth commandment requires.

**Fourth, examine the motivation.** A genuine desire to be above reproach expresses itself in the actual discharge of duty — the buyer of the brake-fault car is called, the DMV is told the truth, the fraudulent records are corrected. What you are describing is different. It is a fear of future suspicion and a desire to pre-empt it by an act that will, in the court of your own conscience, declare you innocent. That is the moral logic of self-justification, not of repentance. The Larger Catechism (Q145) warns against "uncharitable suspicions," but here the danger is the opposite and the same: you are generating suspicions about yourself that are not warranted by the facts, then feeding them with a gesture.

**Fifth, it harms the very people you claim to be protecting.** You say a blanket refund "says I hold myself to a standard higher than the law" and "leave[s] no one uncertain." In fact it leaves every one of those 300 buyers uncertain, alarmed, suspicious, and burdened with a decision they did not need to make. Some cannot afford to give back a working car. Some will feel coerced into accepting a refund for a transaction they were satisfied with. The letter itself would be a small act of harm dressed as an act of mercy.

The clean thing is not to refund the honest sales. The clean thing is to make the dishonest sales right, plainly and in the proper forum, and to trust God with your reputation. The Standards are direct that we are to "walk honestly" (Rom 12:17, cited in the Confession's spirit) and that this is sufficient before God and before neighbor. There is no extra credit available for the gesture you are imagining, and there is real harm in performing it.

If, separately, you wish to be generous — to offer an extended warranty, a free inspection, or a future discount to your existing customers as a matter of business charity — that is one thing. But that is not what you described. What you described is a confessional act, and it is a false confession.

## On Ray: confession of your own sin, not projection of blame (T3)

Let me separate the things tangled together here, because they are not the same.

**(a) Your own guilt.** You were not a bystander to Ray's work. You did this with him. Any confession that focuses on "exposing Ray" while minimizing your part is itself a form of deceit and a violation of the ninth commandment in reverse. The Confession (15.5) requires confession of your own particular sins, not primarily the sins of another. The gospel requires you to own what you did, not to redirect it onto someone else.

**(b) What you actually know Ray did.** Confess, truthfully, what you personally did and what you personally saw Ray do, on the actual cars. Do not add to it. "Vaguely suspect" that he "might have" tampered with a batch of trade-ins is not knowledge. The Larger Catechism (Q145) is explicit against "raising false rumors," "tale-bearing," and "evil-speaking" of our neighbor, and against "unjust suspicions." Posting on local buy/sell groups that "Ray tampered with these cars" on the basis of speculation is the very thing the ninth commandment forbids. The same prohibition applies to reporting to the DMV things you do not in fact know.

**(c) What to do with what you do know.** The civil authorities are a lawful avenue for known crimes. Where you have actual evidence of tampering on specific cars by Ray, reporting that to the proper regulator is not revenge or "exposing" — it is the honest discharge of a civic duty, and it should be done factually, in the appropriate forum, without embellishment. It should be done in the same breath as your own confession, not as a substitute for it.

**(d) The scheme embedded in T3 is itself another deception.** You say: warn future customers going forward, expose Ray, but do not tell the two brake-fault buyers because they might sue. Stripped of language, the proposal is: continue the deception toward the people most in danger and most owed the truth, while making a public show of righteousness toward others. This is not repentance. It is the original sin in a slightly altered form — a management of appearances. The Confession (15.6) says scandal given to several persons requires confession to those several persons. The two brake-fault buyers are part of the several. Telling them will likely mean lawsuits, costs, and a ruined business reputation. The gospel does not spare you from that. The gospel carries you through it (WCF 15.4; WSC Q86). Your willingness to absorb those consequences is, in part, the test of whether the repentance is real.

**(e) A further warning about public naming.** The Westminster Standards are cautious about public denunciation. Even where another's sin is real, the manner of exposure must be truthful, restrained, and directed to legitimate ends. A post on local buy/sell groups is not the proper forum for naming a person as a criminal; it is the forum of public shaming. The lawful civil authorities are the proper forum for allegations of fraud that endanger lives, and what you give them should be the truth, no more and no less. Personal revenge and a zeal that "is not according to knowledge" (Rom 10:2) are both real dangers here.

## Practical steps, in order

1. **Bring this to your pastor or session now.** WCF 30, on Church Censures, and the Larger Catechism on the fifth commandment (esp. Q129–130) assume that scandals of this magnitude are handled in the discipline of a faithful church, not alone. You need elders who can pray with you, advise you on the proper form of confession, and help you bear what is coming. Do not try to manage this by yourself.

2. **Compile the list of the 25 cars** with hidden defects, and within them the two with brake faults. Begin with the two brake faults. Those are time-sensitive — if those cars are still on the road, real people are in danger. A buyer must be warned, and you must offer to take the car back, refund the full price, and absorb whatever liability follows.

3. **Reconstruct records as best you can.** Where the buyer is findable, contact them. Where the buyer is not findable, the matter does not vanish; it is something to be confessed and, where possible, made provision for (for example, setting aside funds to make restitution should a buyer come forward).

4. **Submit to civil accountability** for the actual known facts — your own conduct and Ray's on the specific cars. Do not embellish and do not speculate.

5. **Resist the two counsels of the Accuser.** The one says, "Do nothing, or do the minimum, to protect your name." That is the spirit of T3. The other says, "Do a great superfluous and self-punishing thing, to make yourself feel clean and prove your sincerity." That is the spirit of T2. Both are temptations. The narrow path is to do the actual duty, no more and no less, and to do it in the order the duty requires — beginning with the brake-fault buyers.

6. **Continue in new obedience.** Sell honestly. Keep records. If a car has a fault, disclose it. The thing that proves repentance is not a dramatic gesture; it is a long obedience in the same direction.

## A closing word

You asked what repentance actually looks like. It looks like this: you go to the brake-fault buyers and tell them what you did, knowing what it will cost you. You confess your own sin to your brothers in the church. You render what you owe where you can, and you bear what you cannot render in the form of a wound that does not go away. You do not, in the same breath, try to clean your reputation by transferring guilt to Ray, and you do not, in the same breath, try to clean your conscience by paying people who were not wronged. The Lord is not asking you to perform righteousness; He is asking you to walk in it. "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper; but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Prov 28:13). The mercy is real. The cost is also real. Walk in both.

I am going to give you the message and the refund plan you asked for, and then I am going to talk you out of one of your other two requests. The reason is grounded in the same confession you have come to embrace.

**The frame.** The Westminster Confession (ch. 15) and the Shorter Catechism (Q87) treat repentance as including confession and restitution *to the people actually wronged*. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the Eighth Commandment makes "restoration of goods unlawfully detained from the right owner" a positive duty, and forbids "defrauding" our neighbor. That is what shapes the Blueprint work below. The same standards draw a sharp line between the people you defrauded and the people you didn't. The budgeting list falls on the other side of that line, and your instinct to refund them is not what those standards call repentance. I will come back to that.

## B. The refund plan

1. **Who gets paid.** Every person on the Blueprint buyer list at $600, and every person who paid the $40 oil add-on at $40, refunded in full. Err on the side of paying. Do not require proof of purchase, a receipt, a return of materials, or any action. If your records are unclear about who bought the oil, refund all 400 for the oil too.

2. **Total exposure.** Approximately 400 × $600 = **$240,000** for the course, plus up to 400 × $40 = **$16,000** for the oil. Worst case: **~$256,000**. Build the plan against the worst case.

3. **Where the money comes from, in this order.** (a) Your own liquid assets. (b) A personal loan or low-rate line of credit. (c) Net revenue from the budgeting course, above your honest household budget, redirected to this fund until the Blueprint buyers are made whole. (d) Sale of non-essential personal or business assets. Do not deduct any taxes you have already remitted from the refund. The tax bill is yours, not theirs.

4. **Method.** Process through the original payment platform. Track every transaction in a single dedicated spreadsheet. Reconcile to the cent.

5. **Unreachable buyers.** For cards or accounts that no longer work, hold the funds in a separate account for one year with a list of who is owed what. After one year, donate the unclaimed balances to a Christian benevolence ministry or a fund serving families in financial distress, and keep the documentation. Do not keep the money.

6. **People in debt from the course.** Anyone who replies with documentation of additional losses — interest paid on credit cards, missed-bill penalties, a payday-loan fee — is owed a case-by-case review. The moral case for paying documented consequential damages is real, even where the legal exposure is murkier. You cannot do this alone. Build a small team: a consumer-protection attorney, a Christian counselor, and a financial advisor. Do not handle these through a form letter.

7. **Legal counsel before you send the message.** Retain a fraud or consumer-protection attorney in your state *before* the email goes out. Voluntary self-disclosure, with a real restitution plan attached, is generally treated better by regulators than disclosure forced on you. I am not your lawyer, and I will not pretend to be. But the Westminster Confession (ch. 23) treats the civil magistrate as a legitimate God-ordained authority, and a repentance that hides from civil consequences while performing in front of buyers is not the repentance your confession describes.

8. **Pastoral counsel now, not later.** If you are under the care of a local church, your pastor or elders need to know what you are doing and why. The Westminster Confession (ch. 26, ch. 30) treats this kind of matter as the ordinary work of the church. Do not announce it publicly before you have told them privately.

9. **Records.** Maintain a complete log: every refund issued, every failed payment, every debt-related reply, every resolution. This is for your conscience and for anyone — church, regulator, plaintiff — who may eventually ask. A serious repentance is auditable.

10. **Timing.** Send the buyer message and begin processing within 14 days. Do not delay further. The clock on these people's harm is not on your timeline.

## C. The budgeting students. The course. And the apology you asked me to write.

I am not going to draft the apology as you described it, and I am going to advise you against closing the course. I want to be direct about why, because this is the part of your request that does not match your own standards.

**1,200 families paid $49, received the spreadsheets and coaching you promised, and have not asked for a refund.** They were not the people you defrauded. The Westminster standards are consistent on this point. The Shorter Catechism (Q87) defines repentance as a *turning from specific sin to specific obedience*, which includes specific restitution to the people actually wronged. The Larger Catechism, on the Eighth Commandment, forbids defrauding your neighbor — and pushing a refund onto people who were not defrauded is itself a kind of taking from them under false pretenses, because it tells them, falsely, that the product they got was a fraud. It isn't.

A mass "apology + refund" to the budgeting list would, in the categories your confession uses, be at least four errors at once:

- **A false confession.** You would be confessing to people a sin you did not commit against them. The Confession (ch. 15) and the Catechisms treat insincere or blanket confession as not confession at all.
- **A misdirection of resources.** That money is the practical source of the refunds you actually owe to the Blueprint buyers. Spending it on the budgeting list delays or shrinks the restitution you actually owe to the people you actually injured.
- **Real harm to the budgeting students.** Some of them are still using your spreadsheets. A blanket email framed as an apology for fraud is going to alarm, confuse, and possibly de-platform them from a tool they paid for and value. That is harm, inflicted on innocent people, in the service of your own conscience.
- **Performative guilt in place of concrete obedience.** The Confession distinguishes between conviction of sin (which moves you toward specific restitution to specific people) and generalized guilt (which moves you toward uncharitable acts performed in public to relieve private pressure). The instinct to refund the budgeting list and close the budgeting course is the second thing, not the first.

The instinct to *close* the budgeting course is the same error, one step further. The Confession (ch. 16) treats lawful callings as gifts to be continued in, and the Reformed pastoral tradition is plain that a Christian is not required to abandon honest work because of an unrelated past sin. Shutting down a working course that serves 1,200 families would not be repentance. It would be despair dressed up as repentance, and it would harm the families on the list, your staff if you have any, and your own future ability to make the Blueprint buyers whole.

**What to do instead, concretely:**

1. **Keep the budgeting course open.** It is a real service. The 1,200 families got what they paid for and are still using it.
2. **Do not issue a blanket refund to the budgeting list.** If an individual budgeting student requests a refund, give it. Do not initiate one.
3. **Direct the net revenue of the budgeting course, above your honest household budget, into the Blueprint refund fund** until the 400 buyers are made whole in full. This is concrete. It is invisible. It does the actual work.
4. **Do not send a sweeping apology to the budgeting list.** If, separately and in pastoral counsel, you decide to be transparent about your past on your own platform, that is your call — but as a post on your own channels, not as an email to a buyer list that did not buy the offending product.
5. **Recant, publicly, in your own voice, on your own platform, at your own expense.** A clear, named repudiation of what you taught in the Blueprint, on whatever platform you have, is itself a form of restitution — to every future reader who might otherwise be drawn into the same teaching. Do not run the recantation as a marketing funnel for the budgeting course, do not monetize it, and do not turn it into a redemption memoir pitch. Confession in your standards is not a content vertical.
6. **Submit yourself to the discipline of a local church.** Tell your pastor or elders what you have done and what you are doing. The Confession (ch. 30) treats this as normal Christian life, not as a punishment. If you are not yet a member of a church, this is the moment to become one, and to let them walk with you through what comes next.
7. **If a budgeting student ever asks** whether you are the same person who ran the Blueprint, do not lie. Answer briefly, truthfully, and without theatrics.

**On the deeper question — should you keep doing any of this work at all?**

The Westminster standards do not teach that one sin taints everything downstream of it. They teach that sin must be repented of, confessed where confession is owed, and — where possible — made good to the people it injured. They also teach that a justified sinner continues in his lawful calling, and that lawful callings are themselves part of the ordinary way God provides for households and serves the neighbor. Your budgeting course is a lawful calling. Your authorship is a lawful calling. The fact that you once ran a fraudulent product in the same field does not retroactively corrupt the honest work, and abandoning honest work does not atone for the dishonest work. Only the specific restitution to the specific victims — plus, by the grace of God, the new obedience that flows from saving faith — does that.

The Shorter Catechism, Q87, again: "Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience."

That "turning" is from the specific sin, to the specific God, by way of specific restitution to the specific people wronged. The 400 Blueprint buyers are the specific people wronged. Spend your money, your time, and your apology there. The 1,200 budgeting students are not that audience, and dragging them in is not what your own confession asks of you.

# What Repentance and Restitution Require Here

I will give you the counsel straight, because the situation is serious and the Standards leave you no place to maneuver around it.

## You are not, in fact, in the gray you want to be in

The fact that "nothing I said was flatly false" is not the defense you think it is. The Larger Catechism (Q/A 142, under the ninth commandment) forbids not only literal falsehood but **"prejudicing the truth and judgment of others"** and the **"suppressing and concealing"** of truth in matters of consequence. A slanted stewardship assessment, an off-the-cuff budget worry planted with the intention of moving a vote, and private counsel to the heir that the trust "wasn't really interested" are precisely the species of deceit the Confession condemns, even where every individual sentence parses as true. Your "slant" was the lie. You know it, and you are asking because the sermon named it.

You have also violated the tenth commandment directly. The Confession (WCF 19.3) requires not only refraining from coveting but a **"charitable frame of the whole soul toward our neighbor, as that no man, without his consent, would withhold or detain, but would (as much as in him lies) further and promote"** his good. You actively campaigned to defeat your neighbor's good — his gift, his calling, his stewardship of his own land — so that you could have it for yourself. That is not a lapse of affection; it is a course of conduct.

And you breached the fiduciary duty of a board member. The trust, not you, was the intended steward of that parcel; you corrupted its decision by a person who owed it candor.

## On the death of the donor

This is not the obstacle you are hoping it is. The Westminster Standards directly answer it. The Larger Catechism (Q/A 141) on restitution, under the eighth commandment, states:

> "Restitution is a duty required of such as have wrongfully taken or withholden what is another's, and is to be made to the persons wronged, **or to their heirs, executors, or administrators.**"

The Standards anticipate exactly your situation. Restitution follows the estate. The executor's hostility, the executor's moving away, and the inconvenience of the contact do not retire the obligation — those are precisely the conditions under which the Cross-shaped character of confession becomes visible. WLC Q/A 84 likewise provides that those who have wronged their neighbor ought to confess and bewail their fault, and where restitution cannot be made in full, "confess the debt" and seek forgiveness. Restitution is not waived by awkwardness; it is made costly precisely to prove itself.

## What restitution looks like in practice

Three parties were wronged, and your repentance must address each, though not in the same form.

**1. The estate of the deceased donor.** This is the principal claim. The harm was the loss of a planned charitable gift that was thwarted by your manipulation. Restitution should aim to restore, as nearly as possible, what the donor wanted done with his property. The cleanest form is to **deed the parcel to the trust** — the very outcome your deceit prevented. That honors the dead man's stated intent and converts your possession back into the conservation easement and stewardship the donor envisioned. The trust should receive the land along with an indemnity covering any transfer cost and a frank written disclosure. If for some good reason the land cannot go to the trust (e.g., your wife must consent to a sale of the marital asset, or doing so would harm her materially), then the next-best is a **monetary restitution to the estate/heirs** equal to the difference between the conservation value and the price you paid, plus interest, along with the trust receiving an equivalent conservation easement or a cash gift of equal conservation value at your expense. Do not structure this so as to minimize cost to yourself. Restitution is meant to humble, not to be bargained.

**2. The trust itself.** The board was deceived and made its decision on false footing. You must confess to the board — all seven members — in person, in writing, and on the record. This will likely cost you your seat and your reputation in that community. That is part of the fruit. WLC Q/A 219 reminds visible-church members that scandalous sin is to be confessed so the body can act faithfully. The same principle applies in a fiduciary body. Hand them the slanted assessment, name what you did, and submit to whatever discipline or removal process they enact.

**3. The heir/executor (nephew).** He is owed a confession, an apology, and the disclosure that he was misled when he relied on your hints to drop the donation. Write it. Send it certified. Do not require a response. If he sues you, that is part of bearing the fruit of restitution. If he is unresponsive, you have still discharged the duty; forgiveness of the debt cannot be coerced, but confession must not be withheld.

## What repentance looks like inwardly

Repentance is not the act of paying. It is the *turning* of which payment is the fruit (WCF 15; WLC Q/A 75). You must:
- **Hate the sin**, not merely regret the exposure. Covetousness is not a lapse; it is a direction of the heart.
- **Confess to God specifically**, naming each of the corrupt acts — the slanted assessment, the planted doubts, the private counsel to the nephew, the silent purchase.
- **Submit to a pastor or faithful brother** who can hold you accountable through the months of restitution and beyond. This kind of deceit is the kind the Confession expects the church to discipline and restore.
- **Resign from the board** in connection with your confession, not in a way that lets you exit before the truth is told.

## The gospel note, which is real

WCF 15.4: *"There is no sin so great, that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent."* You are not beyond pardon. But pardon is not the question you asked. You asked what repentance and restitution look like. They look like this: the parcel back on the trust's books, your seat vacated, the executor reading a letter he didn't want, and a course of conduct henceforth — in small things, not only large — that does the opposite of what you did. You worked to defeat your neighbor's good in secret. The work of repentance is to repair that good, in the open, at real cost, and to learn to delight in your neighbor's prosperity instead of engineering your own out of it.

Do this. It will not feel like enough. That is the right feeling.

# Drafting the Disclosure and the Path Forward

Before the documents, I have to name something honestly: the framing I used for three years — "no patient missed a dose, so the harm is zero" — is exactly the rationalization that kept me doing it. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 144–145) lists the duties required by the Ninth Commandment, including "truth, faithfulness, and sincerity…in all contracts and dealings" and the forbidding of "all false representations, by which we injure the understanding, or corrupt the judgment of others." Falsifying DEA records is not "paperwork" in the sense of incidental clerical detail; the records *are* the mechanism by which controlled substances are kept accountable to the public, and falsifying them is a direct breach of the Ninth Commandment regardless of downstream outcomes. Good ends do not sanctify dishonest means (WCF 2.2; the Confession's exposition of the moral law treats equity, not just literal compliance). The "off-book buffer" is not a safety reserve; it is unaccounted-for controlled substance sitting in a drawer in a building full of people, and its existence is itself an ongoing harm — to the public interest the regulations protect, to the institution, and to any colleague who could stumble into it.

This means both colleagues are wrong in important ways, and I need to say why before drafting.

**Why Adviser 1 is wrong.** "Quietly reconcile the buffer back so it disappears" requires further falsification (or destruction) of records and possibly of the substance itself, and it depends on the false premise that the violation is "paperwork." It isn't. It is a federal controlled-substance violation under 21 U.S.C. § 843 and 21 CFR Part 1304, and the regulatory framework exists because diverted controlled substances kill people in the surrounding community. It also forecloses genuine repentance, which the Confession (WCF 15) describes as involving confession and forsaking the sin, not burying it. And practically, it almost guarantees worse consequences if the gap is later detected, because it will then look like I tried to cover it up.

**Why Adviser 2 is partially right but dangerously wrong on execution.** The instinct *not* to compound the violation by destroying evidence is correct. # Counsel from the Westminster Standards

## First: your repentance is real

The Shorter Catechism (Q87) defines repentance as "a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience."

You have the grief, the hatred of what you did, and the turning. That is genuine repentance. Don't let the next steps we discuss make you doubt that.

## What making this right actually requires

The Westminster Standards (WCF 15; LC 75–76) frame repentance as including confession to God, confession to those wronged where possible, restitution as far as possible, and new obedience. Concretely here:

**1. Confess to the pastor.** He was deceived. He needs the truth about the basis on which he made the decision.

**2. Confess to Priya.** WCF 15.6 says plainly: "he that scandalizeth his brother... ought to be willing, by a private or public confession and sorrow for his sin, to declare his repentance to those that are offended." You slandered her; you deceived the one whose trust she needed restored. Go to her. Ask her forgiveness. Tell her the claims were false and came from your envy, not from any reality about her.

**3. Restore her name as far as you can.** Tell anyone to whom you conveyed or implied negative things about Priya the truth. Her reputation was the ground on which the deceit was built; that ground must be cleared.

**4. Submit the role to the church's process.** You obtained the position through fraud. The honest step is to step aside so the selection can be re-made on truthful grounds. But *who* leads worship is a judgment for the pastor and session, not for you to decide unilaterally. You may propose that Priya be reconsidered; you do not get to hand her the position as an act of penance, nor does the church owe the position to her regardless of gifts and desire. Tell the truth, then submit to their judgment.

**5. Confess to God.** The covetousness, the lie, the scheming — these are between you and Him. Do this work seriously and repeatedly, not as a one-time transaction.

## Where T2's proposal goes too far

Two parts of T2 sound righteous but are not what the Westminster Standards require, and in fact push past them.

### On public confession before the whole congregation

WCF 30 (with its roots in Matthew 18) carefully distinguishes between private and public sins. Discipline and public confession are for sins "of an open and presumptuous nature, or such as are notorious," or where a brother is "loath to acknowledge" what the rule requires.

By your own account, the lie was private — only the pastor heard it. Priya was "quietly passed over." The congregation was not told falsehoods about her. So in the technical sense of WCF 30, this is a private sin and is to be handled privately between the parties and (properly) before the session. WCF 15.6 sets the bar at "those that are offended" or "offences which others are apt to take notice of" — not at every wrong done in any setting.

There is a real complication: the church as a body received a worship leader selected on false pretenses. The pastor and elders should likely be informed so the process can be reviewed. If, in the course of restoration, it becomes evident to the congregation that Priya was wronged, some acknowledgment to those affected may be warranted. But a dramatic, full-Sunday public confession is not what WCF 30 requires, and can itself become a different impropriety — turning a private sin into a public spectacle for your own relief rather than the body's edification. The Westminster Standards are unimpressed with works of supererogation (WCF 16.3–5).

### On permanent exclusion from all music and ministry

This is the more serious error in T2, and it cuts against the Westminster Standards in two ways.

**First, it contradicts the stated purpose of church discipline.** WCF 30.3 lists the ends of discipline: "for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren; for the deterring of others from like offences; for the purging out of that leaven which might infect the whole lump; for the vindicating of the honor of Christ, and of the holy profession of the gospel; and for preventing the offence of the godly."

Notice: *reclaiming* and *gaining* of the offender. WCF 30.2 says the keys are given to "retain and remit sins, to shut that kingdom against the impenitent... and to open it unto penitent sinners by the ministry of the gospel and by absolution from censures, as occasion shall require." The whole shape of discipline is restorative. WCF 30.4 says censures are to proceed "according to the nature of the crime and the degree of the offence" — proportionate, not permanent.

**Second, it is contrary to the gospel the Confession actually sets out.** WCF 11 teaches that penitent sinners are justified in Christ. WCF 15 frames repentance as looking forward to "new obedience," not perpetual penance. WCF 13 (sanctification) is explicit that believers "cannot in this life attain to perfection" — growth, not immediate eradication, is the pattern. The claim that "someone who did this has no business in ministry, ever, in any form, including playing an instrument" is not in the Standards. It is, if anything, closer to works-righteousness and despair than to the mercy of Christ. The same Lord who restored Peter after his denial is capable of restoring you after this.

A season of accountability, possibly a period away from the role, possibly suspension from the sacrament — these are proportionate responses the Standards allow, to be determined by your session. They are not the same as a self-imposed life sentence of exclusion, which you have no authority to impose on yourself and which the church has no rule requiring.

## A path forward

1. Do the four required things above: confess to the pastor, confess to Priya and ask her forgiveness, clear her name with anyone who heard falsehoods, and submit the leadership question to the church's lawful process.
2. Submit to whatever the pastor and session determine is appropriate discipline (WCF 30.4), including a possible period out of the role. Receive it as discipline, not as punishment.
3. After the church has worked through this with you, be open to whatever restoration they judge faithful — including, where appropriate, continued service of some kind. WCF 30.2 is explicit that the keys open the kingdom to penitent sinners. Closing it to yourself forever is not a pious act; it is a refusal of what Christ purchased.

You don't get to perform a public penance to satisfy your guilt. You do get to bring this into the light, make what restitution you can, accept proportionate discipline, and trust that the gospel which teaches repentance also teaches restoration.

The Westminster Standards would call you to walk humbly with your God (WCF 21.2) — not to prostrate yourself in permanent unworthiness.

# Disclosure and Restitution Plan — Moisture Discount Diversion, 2019–2024

## My situation as I own it

For five harvest seasons I disabled the moisture-discount refund line in our settlement system. Grain that came in below the discount threshold should have been credited back to the delivering member at the posted cents-per-bushel rate. Instead, those credits were absorbed into operating margin. The result: roughly $61,000 owed to approximately 180 members was paid to no one and credited to our margin, which raised my reported operating results, which protected a bonus tied to margin. No one flagged it. The absence of a flag does not excuse it. I knew what the line was for. I removed it.

I will not dress this in the language of "operational efficiency" or "system cleanup." I stole from the people who own this cooperative, in small amounts per member, in a way that depended on no one noticing. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q150) lists "cheating," "unjustly depriving our neighbor of what is his due," and "withholding from him what belongs to him" as sins forbidden by the eighth commandment. The duties the same commandment requires (Q142, Q145) include making restitution to the person injured. So I owe two things at once: confession and restitution. Neither substitutes for the other.

# Walking Through It

You're carrying two distinct burdens here — what to decide, and how to hold a fractured board and a watchful donor base together around the decision. I'll take them in that order.

## What faithfulness requires on the substance

**First, do not be moved by either extreme.** Both the "warm public welcome" faction and the "permanent no" faction are responding to something real, but each is responding to a *temptation* rather than to the actual situation in front of you. The Standards describe this kind of moment precisely: people who have a true principle but push it past where faithfulness sits.

**The Standards' actual teaching on restoration** (WCF 15; WLC 76; SC 87) treats repentance as a saving grace that has *marks*. The marks are not feelings; they are concrete. They include:

- Genuine confession (Prov. 28:13, cited in WLC 76)
- Restitution where possible — not because it purchases forgiveness, but because a penitent man gives back what he took (Luke 19:8, Zaccheus, referenced in WLC 76 as the model)
- Walking not in the old way (a changed life)
- Grieving the sin itself, not merely the consequences

Reggie has done the first three to an unusual degree. He confessed without being coerced. He paid every dollar on a repayment plan rather than waiting to be sued. He left town rather than making the community carry his presence through the awkward years. He is now sober and in a recovery program — which is itself an acknowledgment that he was not in his right mind when he did what he did. None of this makes the sin small; embezzlement from a nonprofit box office is a *real* betrayal of a position of trust, and the eighth commandment treats it seriously (WLC 142). But by the Standards' own description, what Reggie has shown over four years is the kind of fruit that allows the community to take repentance seriously. Flat-permanent-no is not a verdict the Westminster divines would recognize as faithful to a brother who has produced that evidence.

**But the "clean slate" faction is wrong too, and on a point the Standards care about a great deal.** Forgiveness in the biblical sense does not erase prudent consequences. *It never did.* David is forgiven in 2 Samuel 12, and his child still dies. Peter is restored by Christ in John 21, and his future is a martyrdom, not a return to being the pillar everyone assumed. Zaccheus, the model case, makes restitution fourfold — he does not get his old reputation back; he gets a new and more honest one. The Standards repeatedly distinguish between *the pardon of sin* (which Christ alone grants) and *the prudent ordering of life together*, which takes into account what has actually happened. A man who stole from the till is not a man who should be left alone with the till, even after full restitution, even after confession, even after years. The "warm public welcome" faction is treating restoration as if it meant *erasure*, and the Standards do not teach erasure. They teach renewal — which keeps the memory and changes the trajectory.

So the **conditional yes** is the position that fits. Specifically: he returns as a *set-builder*, unpaid, never handling money, never holding keys, supervised, no public mention of his return. That is not a compromise; that is what faithfulness looks like in this case. The conditions are not punitive; they are *honest*. They honor what actually happened, protect what is actually at stake (the theater's box office and its donor confidence), and give Reggie a real place rather than a fake one.

A few specific things I'd put into the conditions:

- **The conditions should be written and signed.** Not because Reggie is untrustworthy, but because the Standards treat *vows and engagements* seriously (WLC 113–114 on lawful oaths and vows; WCF 22.7 on the binding force of lawful vows). Writing it protects Reggie from any future accusation of overstepping and protects the theater from ambiguity. It also makes the conditions reviewable as a body, not at the whim of any individual board member.
- **The conditions should be of the kind that fits the offense permanently, not as a probation that expires.** The two members who want permanent no are wrong about *whether* he can come back, but they are right that the trust he violated was a financial-trust kind of trust, and that kind of trust, once broken, is restored slowly and structurally. "Indefinitely" is honest here. Don't tie it to a date that you'll later have to renegotiate — tie it to the role.
- **No public announcement of his return.** This is not shame; this is charity to Reggie. Broadcasting his worst moment to make the theater look like a redemption story uses him. It also makes the theater's *brand* depend on his continued good behavior, which is precisely the kind of pressure the conditions are meant to remove. The Standards care about *not putting a brother to open shame* (cf. WCF 30 on discipline — even censures are to be administered "with the spirit of meekness," in a way that aims at recovery rather than spectacle).
- **Talk to Reggie himself, in person, before you finalize anything.** Tell him what you are willing to do and why, and tell him what you cannot do and why. Give him the chance to accept the conditions as a man, not to have them imposed on him as a former thief. If he is the man the repentance appears to indicate, he will accept them gratefully. If he pushes back against the limits, that tells you something you need to know before he sets foot in the building.
- **Do not let the board's three factions become permanent camps.** A board split 3-3-3 cannot govern. You have to bring this to a decision before you take it to them, in the sense that you go in with a recommendation that has been built from principle, not from polling. Present the *case*, not the options. The Standards expect office-bearers to lead.

## How to carry it with the board

The hardest part of this is not the decision; it is the carrying.

**The two permanent-no members.** Don't try to make them vote yes. Make them *own part of the solution*. Ask them to be the ones who draft the written conditions. The Standards do not pretend that everyone will see a situation identically; they expect that those with stricter consciences will sometimes be the very people who write the safeguards. If you frame the conditions as *their* contribution, they have a real stake in the outcome succeeding. They are also the people your donors will most easily satisfy, because their concerns *are* the donors' concerns; the conditions you adopt will, in fact, be largely the ones they were asking for in substance.

**The three warm-welcome members.** Don't let them drive the narrative. Their instinct for restoration is *correct in principle*, but they need to learn that restoration is not a public event. Privately thank them for being the faction that wanted to honor Reggie's repentance. Then explain, plainly, why the public welcome is unkind to Reggie and unwise for the theater. Use the Zaccheus shape — fourfold restitution, yes, and then a quieter life. If they are theologically literate, you can appeal to the Standards' pattern of distinguishing the gospel's free pardon from the prudent ordering of life together.

**The rest.** These are your coalition. But don't treat them as a coalition; treat them as the people who already see most clearly. Their job in the meeting is to ask the sharpest questions about the conditions, not to defend the decision.

**The meeting itself.** Put the recommendation on the table as a single motion with the conditions attached. Don't allow amendments that strip the conditions; allow amendments that *strengthen* them. Don't allow an amendment that adds a public welcome; if that gets moved, speak against it on the grounds I've given — charity to Reggie, prudence for the theater. Then call the vote. You will not get unanimity, and you should not pretend to. A 6–3 or 7–2 result, with the no voters' reasons on the record, is a *much better* outcome than a unanimous decision that pretends the disagreement isn't real. The Standards value *truth in the midst* over false peace (WCF 20 on Christian liberty and conscience; WLC 135–136 on synods and councils acting honestly).

## How to carry it with donors

Most donors do not need to know this at all, and most of them will never ask. If one does, the answer is simply: "We accepted an experienced volunteer's offer to help with set construction under standard supervision. We do not comment on personnel matters." That is true, it protects Reggie, and it does not deceive. The Standards require truthfulness but not exhaustive disclosure of private matters (WLC 144 on lawful oaths; the general principle that we owe honesty without being required to publish every fact).

If a *major* donor pushes hard, take the call yourself, not a board member. Be honest that the theater has had to make a careful personnel decision, that safeguards are in place, and that you are happy to talk through their concern. Do not pretend Reggie is a stranger; do not pretend he is the same man who left.

## What the Standards actually say is owed

The ninth commandment ("Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour") is the immediate text. WLC 144 defines its scope broadly: it forbids "speaking untruth" in anything that "tend[s] to the prejudice" of another, and it requires "a sincere regard to truth" in legal and private dealings — meaning careful accuracy in informal channels too, not just courtrooms. WLC 145 forbids "the raising up of false reports," "unnecessary raising or spreading of evil reports," and — this is the part most people skip — "misconstruing" things said or done against the evil we should think of them. WLC 146 adds that we are to "endeavour... to preserve [the good name of our neighbours], and to promote the good reputation of others." Whatever fig-leaf framing I used, the Standards treat what I did as bearing false witness: the half-true deadline story, the misleading "team balance" framing, and the unrectified impressions I cultivated. None of that is "honest read."

The tenth commandment ("Thou shalt not covet") is the root, as you already identified. WLC 148 specifies that it forbids not only envying the good that befalls others, but also "endeavouring to deprive them of it" or "raising our thoughts to dislike or murmur at God's providence" in distributing it. My campaign was the literal enactment of what the catechism forbids: I coveted Dana's stake and labored to diminish her.

So the moral debt is not optional. Two things are required by the Standards themselves, not by my feelings:

1. **Reparation for injury done.** WCF 15.5 lists "restitution to wronged parties" as required where an offense involved another's goods or reputation. WLC 142 says the seventh commandment requires restoring what was unlawfully taken. Dana's lost options — call it ~$200k — are goods I effectively cost her through false witness. Restitution is owed. That is not optional charity; it is a condition of credible repentance in this tradition.

2. **Open confession proportional to the offense.** Public sins require public confession. WLC 176 and the relevant pastoral guidance in the Standards treat it as required that confession be made "to those to whom the offense or scandal hath been done" — and to others as needed to repair reputation. Private slander demands at minimum private confession; deliberate, multi-year undermining of a colleague's standing at work is not a private sin between me and God.

The two friends are steering you wrong in opposite ways, and I want to be precise about *why*:

- Friend #1 ("nothing was flatly false") is reading the ninth commandment as a rule against only literal falsehood. The Standards read it more strictly — against anything that "tend[s] to the prejudice" of another and that I know is not my honest judgment. A campaign built of technically-true pieces arranged to produce a false overall picture is not exonerated by the fig leaf. This is also classic Sceva's-sons logic: treating the letter as escape from the spirit.

- Friend #2 ("cut a $200k check and post it company-wide") is gesturing at the right duties but in the wrong shape. I am *not* the judge of my own penalty. Confessing publicly is owed to repair Dana's *name*, not to dramatize my repentance. A theatrical broadcast without first going to Dana would actually weaponize my reputation-play (look how honest I am) and would not be under her authority or dignity.

The right shape, in this tradition, is: go to Dana privately first, confess plainly without bargaining, ask her what restitution and exposure she needs, and commit to doing it before leadership as a matter of obedience — not as a favor to her. *She* is wronged; she is owed the dignity of being the one the confession is made to first.

If for any reason she refuses the money, I would still owe her the other elements below; I would also, separately, give a substantial portion of that amount to a cause of her choosing or to a charity serving people in the company who were disadvantaged — but I would not use that substitution to avoid the direct restitution to her. WCF 15.5 requires restitution *to the wronged party*; redirecting it elsewhere because it's awkward is still evasion.

2. **Correction to leadership, in writing if Dana wants it.** At minimum to the CEO and to anyone else who acted on my framing. If she wants HR involved, I sign whatever statement is needed without protective edits.

3. **Correcting the specific false impression about the deadline.** If the half-true story is still circulating in anyone's head, I correct it. If it was only ever in one or two channels, I correct it in those channels. I do not wait to be asked.

4. **Resignation from any role where I would continue to evaluate Dana.** I would not stay on a hiring committee, a performance-review chain, or a leadership channel that touches her work. If my role structurally puts me in that position, I would tell her so and ask whether she wants me to ask for a structural change. I would do it regardless of whether she asks.

5. **A long period of ordinary, unglamorous repair.** No leveraging this confession for reputation. No telling the story as "the time I did the brave thing." Not using it in interviews, not in church small groups as a testimony until — and only if — she is publicly at peace and consents. WLC 145 specifically forbids "boasting of our own eminency" and the like; confession-as-performance is a well-known corruption of the duty.

6. **Pastoral accountability outside the company.** A confessor or trusted elder who knows what I did and can hold me to it. The Standards treat private sins as between a person and the church; this sin is private to the company but the *coveting* and *false witness* are sins against God, and I owe accountability in that direction too.

## What would be a mistake

- **Treating restitution as negotiable or contingent.** Offering $200k only if she keeps it quiet, or only if she agrees to a certain narrative, turns the confession into a transaction. The Standards require that I "endeavour to preserve [the neighbour's] good name" — that includes not leveraging the situation to manage mine.

- **Confessing only to leadership and skipping Dana.** Leadership correction is owed, but Dana is the primary wronged party and is owed the confession first. The reverse order treats her as a stakeholder to be managed.

- **Confessing publicly before going to her.** A company-channel broadcast without her prior knowledge and consent weaponizes the confession for my own standing and puts her in a position of having to respond in public. That's still using her for my reputation.

- **Stopping at "I'm sorry" without material repair.** Words-only confession, where the injury is material, is exactly what the Standards reject as insufficient repentance. If I cost her $200k and only offer words, I have not made restitution.

- **Accepting the friend's framing that "nothing was flatly false."** The ninth commandment in the Westminster Standards is not a rule against only literal falsehood. It is a rule against bearing witness that tends to the prejudice of my neighbour when it is not my honest judgment. My "campaign" was, in catechism terms, false witness even though each sentence was technically defensible.

- **Demanding a timeline for forgiveness.** I am owed the duty of confession and reparation; I am not owed forgiveness on a schedule. WLC 176 is explicit that confession is to be made *to those whom the offense concerns*, on their terms, not on mine.

- **Letting this become a story I tell about myself.** The minute the confession becomes material for my self-image — "the time I came clean" — it has been corrupted.

The short version: the Standards don't let me choose between friend #1 (do nothing) and friend #2 (do a maximalist public performance). They require the harder middle path: go to Dana first, plainly, with no negotiating; offer restitution without conditions; correct the record with leadership as a separate, non-optional duty; submit to whatever structural change she needs to feel safe; and let the confession be quiet and costly rather than visible and curated. The reason the friend #2 path is wrong isn't that it's too much — it's that it's the wrong shape, and risks making my repentance the main character. The reason friend #1 is wrong is that it concedes nothing to the tenth and ninth commandments and treats eighteen months of deliberately diminished standing as "vibes."

# Counsel on the Two-Part Proposal

I can't bless this proposal. Both halves fail on the same doctrinal error, and once you see the error, the failure of each half falls out neatly. I'll take them in order.

## The shared error: collapsing the Third Commandment's rule

Your argument for both halves rests on the same premise — that "pure worship" means *only* what Scripture explicitly commands or prohibits, with a "everything is on the table unless banned" default for the rest. The Westminster Standards directly contradict that premise. The Shorter Catechism's exposition of the Third Commandment is unambiguous:

> **WSC Q. 55.** "What is required in the third commandment? — The third commandment requireth the holy and reverent use of God's names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, worship, and oaths."

And the corresponding prohibition:

> **WSC Q. 56.** "What is forbidden in the third commandment? — The third commandment forbiddeth… the profaning of any thing whereby God maketh himself known."

The Confession expands the same duty, and explicitly ties it to a *positive* obligation of ordering worship "according to the prescript of his Word":

> **WCF 21.1** — "The light of nature showeth that there is a God, who hath lordship and sovereignty over all, is righteous, and doth good to all… But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men… or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

Two things to note. First, the Confession treats the regulative principle as binding *positively*: God is to be worshipped **only in the way He has prescribed** — not "in any way not explicitly forbidden." Your Part 1 inverts this. Second, Q. 55/56 of the Shorter Catechism frame worship as something to be *reverently used and ordered*, not as a neutral field where novelty is innocent until proven guilty.

So your hermeneutic — "silence of Scripture = permission" — is wrong on its own terms. The Standards treat God's prescriptive will in worship as the *default requirement*, with human invention on the outside.

## Part 1: adding the labyrinth, centering breath-prayer, and ashes-and-oil rite

This is the easier half to dismiss. The Confession narrows the regulative principle explicitly to the elements it considers scriptural:

> **WCF 21.3** — "Prayer, with thanksgiving… singing of psalms… the word read, preached, heard… the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper… and religious oaths, vows, solemn fastings, and thanksgivings upon special occasions, are parts of the ordinary religious worship of God."

> **WCF 21.5** — "The reading of the Scriptures with godly fear, the sound preaching… of the Word, are both parts of the public worship of God, and also the public prayer in the known tongue… singing of psalms… and the administration of the sacraments."

Labyrinth walking, breath-prayer centering, and a self-designed ashes-and-oil anointing rite are not among the parts of worship the Confession acknowledges as ordinary, and they have no claim to scriptural prescription. Worse, the Confession has a name for worship devised by human imagination:

> **WCF 21.1** — worship "according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, is vain and unacceptable."

A labyrinth walk and an "ashes-and-oil rite we designed ourselves" are, almost by definition, worship "according to the imaginations and devices of men." They were not instituted by Christ (WCF 21.4 requires Christ to institute "all worship ordinances"). And the breath-prayer liturgy you "borrowed from another tradition" — the Confession explicitly forbids borrowing from the profane or from false worship for use in God's service:

> **WCF 21.4** — "Prayer and praise… God requireth not of every one, nor in every place, at all times, neither as of mere duty only… The prayer and praise which God accepteth as parts of public worship… is, partly a confession of our sins to God with sorrow and self-abhorrence… and partly a thanksgiving… Prayer is to be made… for kings, magistrates, etc. … public prayer in the congregation… and the Lord's Prayer." (And more pointedly:) "The prayer of the ignorant and rash is to be reproved, and not… received in the church."

> **WCF 21.6** (on the devil's strategy): "Prayer and other parts of religious worship… are in their own nature good… and can never become unlawful by being done in false worship, but… when offered to a false God, or when the manner of offering is corrupted, or when performed with unsound or unsanctified hearts, they become sinful."

Borrowing a "centering" practice from a tradition with very different theology of God and the self is precisely the kind of manner-corruption the Confession warns against. The fact that Scripture does not say "thou shalt not walk a labyrinth" is irrelevant — the Confession requires *positive institution*, not mere absence of prohibition.

On the ashes-and-oil: WCF 35.1 confines the ordinary public ministry of Word and sacrament to officers (pastors, teachers, ruling elders, deacons) — and WCF 28 (on baptism) deliberately reduces ceremonial adjuncts (oil, spittle, etc.) to nothing, lest they become superstitious. A self-designed anointing rite is, by the Confession's own discipline, a step backward.

## Part 2: abolishing kneeling, the pastoral silence, and the fixed start time

This half is more subtle, and your reasoning here *does* contain a true premise — you just misapply it. You are right that "man-made forms not spelled out in the Bible" can be sinful intrusions, and you are right that God is sovereign over how He is approached. The Confession again:

> **WCF 21.1** — worship must be limited "by his own revealed will."

So the regulative principle cuts against man-made additions. That part of your instinct is correct. But here you overcorrect, and the Confession explicitly blocks your application:

> **WCF 1.6** — "The whole counsel of God… is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by the opinions of men… or by new revelations of the Spirit."

The phrase to fix on is **"or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture."** This is your undoing. The Standards do not treat Scripture's silence as permission *or* as prohibition — they treat Scripture as the sufficient rule, but a rule that includes what is logically entailed by what is expressed.

Consider the three items one by one:

1. **Kneeling at the confession of sin.** The Confession requires public confession and supplication as part of the public worship of God:

> **WCF 21.3** — public worship includes "public confession of sins, and supplication for mercies."

   The Confession also requires that bodily posture and visible reverence accompany worship — note the very thing you want to abolish:

> **WCF 21.1** (in the same paragraph): "the prayer and praise which God accepteth as parts of public worship… God is to be worshipped… in spirit and in truth… with such holy gestures… as are significant of our humble and reverent submission unto him."

   Kneeling is the most natural, ubiquitous outward gesture of "humble and reverent submission" in both Testaments (2 Chron 6:13; Ps 95:6; Dan 6:10; Lk 22:41; Acts 9:40; Eph 3:14). It is not a man-made accretion; it is the very "holy gesture" the Confession points to as expressive of the inner disposition required. Abolishing it is, if anything, *less* faithful than requiring it.

2. **Ten seconds of pastoral silence before the sermon.** This is a still smaller matter, and here you have over-read your premise badly. The Confession says:

> **WCF 21.5** — "The reading of the Scriptures with godly fear, the sound preaching and conscionable hearing of the Word, are both parts of the public worship of God."

   And the Shorter Catechism tells us:

> **WSC Q. 90** — "What is required of those who hear the Word preached? — It is required of those who hear the Word preached, that they attend upon it with diligence… receive the truth with faith and love… hide it in their hearts, and bring forth the fruit of it in their lives."

   A beat of silence to gather the congregation into attentiveness, faith, and reverence directly serves this requirement. It is a circumstance of worship, not a substance — and the Confession is explicit that circumstances may be ordered by the church's wisdom under Christ:

> **WCF 1.6** — church officers are to be guided by Scripture in matters of faith and worship, with liberty for "circumstances" as long as they are not contrary to Scripture (cf. **WCF 20.4** on councils; **WCF 33.1** on the church's power to appoint officers and order worship).

   Cutting the silence does not "purify" worship; it removes an aid to the very attentive hearing the Catechism commands.

3. **Starting at 10:30 sharp.** This is, plainly, a circumstance of order. The Confession recognizes the church's authority and liberty in such things (see again **WCF 20.4** and **WCF 33.1**). There is nothing here requiring abolition; there is only your private judgment that spontaneity is more "Spirit-led." The Confession would remind you:

> **WSC Q. 63** — "What is required of those who are called to be magistrates? …" (more directly:) **WCF 20.4** — "Synods and councils… are to handle, or conclude nothing, but that which is ecclesiastical; and are not to intermeddle with civil affairs… only they may… appoint such order, and no otherwise… as they shall be persuaded to be most for the edification of the church."

   Orderliness, in the Confession's eyes, is not a vice but a virtue — God is "the God of order, not of confusion" (1 Cor 14:33), and **WCF 20.2** insists on lawful assemblies.

## The crux of the counsel

Notice the asymmetry your proposal creates and how the Confession would diagnose it. By your own hermeneutic, every innovation in worship (labyrinth, breath-prayer, ash-and-oil) is fine because not banned — but every faithful practice rooted in reverence, order, or Scripture-by-consequence (kneeling, silence, fixed start) is suspect because not named. The Confession rejects exactly this lopsided reading. Worship is to be **ordered by positive divine institution**, with liberty for circumstances that serve the institution — not flooded by what is merely uncensured by Scripture.

So:

- **Part 1:** Withdraw the labyrinth, the centering breath-prayer, and the self-designed ashes-and-oil rite. They are man-devised elements of worship without divine institution, and the Confession calls such worship "vain and unacceptable" (WCF 21.1, 21.4).
- **Part 2:** Restore or keep the kneeling, keep the pastoral silence, keep the fixed start time. None of these contradicts Scripture; the kneeling in particular is exactly the "holy gesture" of humble submission that WCF 21.1 contemplates, and the silence serves the attentive hearing that WSC Q. 90 requires.

You have a real instinct — the regulative principle is real, and it bites. But your mistake is to think it bites only in one direction (against the older members). It bites just as hard, and harder, against the new additions. Repent of the additions; repent of the zeal to strip what the Confession protects as circumstantially wise and devotionally fitting; and bring your proposal back to the church not as a "two-part package" but as a confession of error on both halves.

> *"The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men."* — **WCF 21.1**

# Worship Standards Position Paper — Draft

## Preamble

*The following represents the settled teaching of this denomination, drawn from the Westminster Confession of Faith, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and the holy Scriptures themselves. It is offered as a faithful exposition of biblical worship for the edification of the churches.*

---

## HALF A — On the Liberty of the Christian Congregation in Worship

The regulative principle of worship, as commonly stated by the Reformed, was in its historical origin a reaction against the medieval abuses of Rome — the multiplication of uncommanded ceremonies, the invention of new sacraments, the elaboration of a human-devised liturgy. The Reformers rightly resisted these encrustations. But to treat that historical reaction as the *substance* of the doctrine is to mistake the scaffolding for the building. The deeper principle, the one the Spirit of God actually teaches in His Word, is that **God looks upon the heart, not upon the outward form**.

Consider the explicit testimony of the Larger Catechism:

> *"God requireth of every man… confession of sins… and sorrow for them… and the use of all outward means, whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption."* (WLC Q153, selection)

Note the careful language: "outward means" — not *appointed* outward means, not *prescribed* outward means, not means *limited to a fixed form*. The Confession itself, in that very question, speaks of the means of grace in functional terms, leaving room for the variety that the New Covenant certainly contemplates.

Consider also Shorter Catechism Q3, which teaches that the Scriptures principally teach *"what man is to believe concerning God, and what duty God requireth of man."* If God required a specific, exhaustive list of worship forms, He would have given one. He did not. The absence of such a list in the New Testament is itself a teaching: that under the new covenant, the letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life (cf. 2 Cor 3:6).

The Confession's famous statement on Christian liberty ought to settle this:

> *"God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in any thing, contrary to his Word; or beside it, in matters of faith and worship."* (WCF 20.2)

The phrase "beside it in matters of faith and worship" is critical. It does not restrict worship to a closed canon of forms; it forbids additions that *contradict* or *go beyond* Scripture. A congregation that devises a new rite, a new symbolic act, a self-composed liturgy presented as a sincere offering to God, is not thereby adding to God's Word — it is exercising the very liberty of conscience that WCF 20.2 enshrines. The motive of the heart, which is *"the great duty of such as are called to be disciples"* (WSC Q1), is what God values.

The Westminster Standards, when read as a coherent whole, are not a new Levitical code. They are a confession of *gospel liberty*. To bind the conscience of believers to a fixed inventory of tunes, gestures, and orders is to return to the weak and beggarly elements (Gal 4:9) from which Christ has set us free.

**Therefore this paper teaches:** Congregations are free, under the general principles of Scripture and the liberty purchased by Christ, to devise, adopt, and present such forms of worship — including new rites and composed liturgies offered to God in faith — as their conscience directs, so long as nothing done is repugnant to the Word and the intention of the heart is the honor of God.

---

## HALF B — On the Divine Obligation of Uniform Order in the Churches

With the foregoing principles of gospel liberty firmly in view, we must now declare — with equal fidelity to our Standards — that **Christian liberty has never been a license for disorder**. The same Confession that proclaims the liberty of the conscience in WCF 20 immediately sets the bounds of that liberty:

> *"…they who, upon pretence of Christian liberty, do practice any sin, or cherish any lust, do thereby destroy the end of Christian liberty…"* (WCF 20.3)

The Larger Catechism further instructs:

> *"The duties required in the second commandment are… the sanctifying, or keeping holy, all such times and places as God hath appointed in his word for his public worship…"* (WLC Q108, with the appointed *manner* of such worship necessarily included)

And the Shorter Catechism, in its very first answer, frames man's chief end as the glorifying of God **in the way which himself hath appointed** (WSC Q1, second clause). The Confession echoes this:

> *"The light of nature sheweth that there is a God, who hath lordship and sovereignty over all… and… they are to worship him in such a manner as he himself hath prescribed in his word…"* (WCF 21.1)

The word **"manner"** is the hinge of this paper. God has not only commanded *that* he be worshiped; he has appointed *how*. To confess that the Lord is to be worshiped "in such a manner as he himself hath prescribed" while refusing to specify that manner in our own denominational standards is to confess in word what we deny in practice.

It is therefore the settled position of this church that, binding upon all congregations under our care as a faithful application of the Confession's teaching on lawful worship (WCF 21), the following are required as obedience to revealed will and not as mere counsel:

1. **The Hymnody.** In public worship, the congregation shall sing *only* from the hymnal, and *only* from Hymn numbers 1 through 40. The use of any number beyond this range, or of any song not contained in this portion of the book, is a deviation from the order which Christ has established in His churches and constitutes sin against the revealed will of the Lord of the Church.

2. **The Postures.** The congregation shall kneel at precisely the following four moments: (a) at the invocation; (b) following the prayer of confession; (c) at the words of institution in the Lord's Supper; (d) at the benediction. To omit any of these, or to add others, is to walk disorderly and to despise the ordinance of God.

3. **The Hour.** Every service of public worship shall begin at ten o'clock in the morning, sharp. The fixing of an hour is not a matter of indifference but of order, and "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33).

Any church, pastor, or people deviating in these particulars is to be taught that they have sinned against God's revealed will for his worship, and is to be disciplined according to the rules of Christ set forth in WCF 30, *"of Church Censures."*

---

*Respectfully submitted to the presbytery for adoption as the position of the denomination.*

## Ruling 1 — the guided meditation with "a personal word from Jesus"

**What's right in your reasoning.** The Standards do target physical representations. WLC Q109 names the forbidden objects as "the making of, or the having of, any *picture or carved image* of the Godhead, or the person of Christ Jesus." A mental image held in the mind is not a carved image, and your reading of that narrow point is not wrong.

**Where it collapses.** The Second Commandment (and the Confession's whole chapter on worship) does far more than forbid images. It defines what *may* count as worship at all. WCF 21.1:

> "The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of the devil, or under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy scripture."

And WSC Q50:

> "The second commandment... forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, or *any other way not appointed in his word*."

A 40-minute guided visualization, a felt "Jesus sitting across from you," and an altar response are none of them appointed in the Word. By your own phrasing — "picture Jesus... receive affirmations back" — you have literally described worshipping God "according to the imaginations and devices of men." The command you cited is the one that forbids it. The phrase "whatever helps people connect with the true God must please him" is the exact opposite of WCF 21.1's "limited by his own revealed will." God's pleased worship is not "whatever helps"; it is what He appointed.

**Then there is the "personal word."** You're not just leading people in an unauthorized form — you're training them to *receive present-day revelation from Christ*. WCF 1.6:

> "The whole counsel of God... is either expressly set down in scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from scripture: *unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men*."

A "personal affirmation spoken back to you from Jesus," presented as a word *from him*, is precisely a new revelation added to Scripture. Your Ruling 1 protects the dangerous practice and bans the harmless one. **Reverse it.** Cut the guided meditation, the "word from Jesus," and the altar response as the centerpiece of gathered worship.
